title: Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers
body_text: Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers Models Benchmarks Chat Rankings Apps Ori Pricing Docs Models Benchmarks Chat Rankings Apps Ori Pricing Docs Light mode Blog / Announcements / Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers On this page Provider security announcements Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers OpenRouter · 11/22/2026 Provider security announcements Provider security announcements Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld. We have been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them. These findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter. The results of this testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers. A live list of the security announcements we have received from providers is below . As the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers, we take data policy enforcement very seriously. We have taken the following actions: Off-boarded three providers from OpenRouter, based on the results of our investigations. Removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility. The removals included providers flagged by researchers, plus additional endpoints that we removed as a precautionary measure. Notified all potentially affected customers. The following work is underway: We are adapting the researchers’ testing approach so we can run these checks on an ongoing basis. We are conducting technical verification of network paths to identify instances where requests and responses may be being forwarded to third parties. We are requiring appropriate assurances and validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any endpoint removed in this review. We are grateful for the Dragos report. As we integrate similar testing techniques into OpenRouter, we will keep raising the bar, and providers that want to be on OpenRouter will need to meet it. Provider security announcements Atlas Cloud: Our commitment to your security and privacy Novita: Privacy notice regarding MiniMax requests on Novita Phala: November preliminary incident report Together: Security event: prompt leakage for requests in June and July of 2026 Not all affected providers have posted publicly. We have notified affected users regardless of whether there is a public post. We are encouraging all providers to create incident write-ups and will keep this list updated. title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
body_text: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS | The Mozilla Blog Skip to content Mozilla Internet Culture Life Online Deep Dives Q&As Firefox Privacy & Security Firefox Features Tips and Tricks Firefox AI Mozilla VPN New Products Advertising Principles Our Work Internet Policy From the Team Download Firefox Search Search for: Internet Policy Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS November 20, 2026 Mozilla Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone. But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.  This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox. As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.     Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test. Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.  One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step. That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.   The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.  Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor. Previous Post Has Microsoft wronged you? title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
body_text: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH | Math 216: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry Home About AGITTOC 2020 2011-12 course 2014 course 2015-16 course 2017-18 course Math 216: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry November 20, 2026 Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH Posted by ravivakil under Uncategorized Leave a Comment   Updated November 22, 2026: The story so far: Alessandro Maria Masullo has a proposed proof of GRH, and Brian Conrad has been looking closely at it for months and gave extensive feedback which is being incorporated, and it was so far looking good to him. It is all human, with no AI. The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current version, in the state that it happens to be in (mid-revision). Yesterday, in the midst of meetings, I hurriedly posted it, writing: “I hope people quickly check it, formalize, fill any small gaps if they occur. I really hope it works. I have great faith in Brian’s judgement, and Brian has put a lot of thought into checking what Alessandro has done. There is a long story to tell, but right now I want to get the file out. Here it is.” About 8 hours later I updated: “I’m out of the meetings, and now catching up! Several people have contacted me to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. (Thanks to several mathematicians in particular who were first to let me know.) As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)” Links (including the draft), at which further updates can hopefully be found: John Baez and Álvaro Lozano-Robledo . This will probably be my final update on the subject, barring major new developments. For future questions about the mathematics, please contact Brian Conrad; I haven’t yet had the chance even to look at Masullo’s document, having just received it Friday (and in any case, it is out of my expertise). These are exciting times, and I look forward to the acceleration of mathematical discovery continuing! title: Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do?
body_text: Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do? | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do? 727 points by LetThingsBeDiff 2 days ago | hide | past | favorite | 825 comments I'm Senior software engineer in the US (DMV area), with 15y of experience. Worked for Fortune 50+ company and bunch of mid-size companies. Been unemployed for 2y and can't find a job, within those 2 years, I pretty much spent my savings that I've saved through years, maybe have 4-5 months left to support my household. Currently, I tutor math and probably about to start working as manager in pizzaria. In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE. At this point, I have massive gap in my resume that I can't explain to recruiters, I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI, but who cares if date of my last employment is Jan2025. What should I do ? If you have an alternative path (something completely different from SWE or SWE adjacent) that pays "well", I would like to hear.   help powvans 1 day ago | next [–] > In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE. I don't know the OP's circumstances. What I am about to say is meant as advice to others and not a criticism of the OP. If you suspect that you may be the target of a layoff, DO NOT SIMPLY QUIT. In this scenario you are a potential liability to your employer. They will almost certainly pay you to leave if they decide to part ways. It is always easier to find a job when you have a job. Maybe you think if there are layoffs and you are retained that it will be a miserable working environment. Fine. DO NOT QUIT. After a round of layoffs you are relatively safe and you can use that time to find another job. It is very likely that layoffs are going to continue as companies restructure because of AI. Have a plan. Keep your wits and hold fast. reply al_borland 14 hours ago | parent | next [–] There are also companies that do layoffs routinely. When I started where I work, they didn't. I remember the first time I experienced layoffs, it was a dark day in the office. These days, they happen at least twice per year, and that's been the trend for many years now. I've been at the company for over 2 decades now, and have watched countless rounds of layoffs happen while I retained my job. Never actually feeling like you have job security when being somewhere for 20 years is not fun, but it does highlight that they aren't always the end. On year, I was told 3 times I was getting laid off, I had meetings with HR and signed severance papers and everything... as I left the office my boss told me not to worry... that was 10 years ago. I'm still working there, that boss was laid off a few years later. It could be that companies that historically didn't do layoffs are starting to move into the regular cadence I've been experiencing for years. To echo the parent, I don't know OP's situation, but these scenarios exist. reply gmmachine 1 hour ago | root | parent | next [–] I was in a department that operated like that. This philosophy, of an ever present Damoclesian layoff, it comes from Jack Welch right? Why hire someone in the first place just to lay them off? That's what we should ask as labor. reply mrbonner 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] I was reading that line and wondering the same thing. I know OP may feel pride and such (I would too). reply vigilantpuma 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Pride? Where is the shame in being laid off? reply ChuckMcM 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Well, in my experience that regardless of how its done, when the company asks you to leave and continues on without you, it feels like they fired you and that you were not "picked" to continue on with them. If the company dissolves after laying you off that is a different thing. For employees its a double negative, new employers will see being laid off as "you weren't part of the top 10%" and by leaving on your own terms, "this guy's a quitter, he might quit on us too." Which is really just people trying to find excuses to not hire. When I was on the hiring rotation at Google I asked the committee once "Why do you bring these people in if you already don't think you will hire them?" The whole "Maybe they will surprise us..." rings hollow. My advice to the folks like the OP living in the US is to use your IT experience to help folks in Active Senior kinds of communities with their IT issues. You can do it for 'free' or a nominal charge. This is an easy way to network with successful former executives who still have contacts in the industry. reply eloisant 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] > new employers will see being laid off as "you weren't part of the top 10%" No that's not the case. There are many reasons your employer decide you're the one the be laid off that are not related to performances. Maybe your salary is higher. Maybe your whole department or location is shutdown. New employers know that and don't judge laid off people. > this guy's a quitter, he might quit on us too. That can be true, but only if you have a short tenure in the companies you worked for. Companies might think that if you have multiple jobs with less than a year. But if you quit a company after working for at least 2/3 years, companies won't judge you for that. reply Plasmoid 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] > New employers know that and don't judge laid off people. While nothing is universal, there are lots of companies that will absolutely not hire someone who has been laid off on the basis that they are the "scraps" or "they were cut for a reason". It's awful but it's not exactly uncommon. reply tibbar 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Yes. Unfortunately, in a previous job I saw candidates with stellar resumes, interview results, and references blocked from an offer because they were part of a layoff in the past. It was shocking to me at the time, but it definitely happens. reply cebert 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] There should be laws against this reply Pokepokalypse 21 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Laws against having an opinion, even if it's wrong? How do you even enforce that? reply allarm 8 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Several examples come to mind of opinions that are not viewed favorably by society or by the laws of several countries. reply vigilantpuma 10 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] You know there are already a bunch of things that you can’t use to discriminate against people in employment, right? reply monksy 23 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] But we all live in America. Where the government and private controllers don't want workers to be independent. reply smackeyacky 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I would agree with this. Seeing a new org chart without your name stings quite a bit reply vigilantpuma 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] I know it’s PAINFUL to beaid off. I have that experience firsthand (and while I was on maternity leave to boot)! But I was never ashamed to be laid off. reply rpdillon 11 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Depends on whether or not you think that new org chart has any chance of achieving its goals. I always imagined that getting laid off would feel like treading water in the ocean while you watch the ship sail on, but if you're in a life raft and the ship is sinking, I can imagine it feeling quite a bit different. reply ulfw 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Who gets shown an org chart after not working at the company anymore?! reply smackeyacky 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] This was a particularly dysfunctional company. reply f3408fh 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] You just spent a few paragraphs explaining how unfair and arbitrary the hiring process is, as a former employee of one of the most prestigious companies in the world. And your proposed solution boils down to “Maybe if you fix the right retired millionaire's Wi-Fi, they'll put in a good word for you.” reply ChuckMcM 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Personally, I don't think your re-worded version is much better. When you, f3408fh, become unemployed, what do you do? Hmmm? This is consistent, "Networking is the single most effective way to find work, and the evidence has been consistent on this for decades." Which is great, when you're working, and sucks if you're trying to build a network now that you aren't working. I recognize that I benefited from a massive amount of privilege. I'm white, I'm male, I'm in an area where there are hundreds of companies that do work that needs the skills of someone like me and I'm weird in that I enjoy doing technical work even if I don't get paid for it. But when I left my job at Sun Microsystems after nearly 10 years there I realized I didn't know anybody. Sure, I knew people who I had worked with, and I could tell you what they worked on at Sun, but their spouse's name? Their favorite hobby / sport? What sort of movies they liked? I wasn't friends, by any definition of friends, with any of them. I set out to change that and from that period forward. I engaged with the lives of people I worked with in order to better know them and they could better know me. Not everyone wants to be friends, fine. But for folks who I was friends with they could reach out when they needed help and I could reach out when I needed help. That made it easier, maybe even possible, for me to get employed in technical roles when I was over 50. That may not be true anymore in this world of AI scanned resumes and company spanning ATS systems, but it sure made a difference in my life. The folks I knew who couldn't get hired correlated strongly with people who didn't go to the company social events or have any sort of relationship with their coworkers. That's a valid choice, my observation was that the cost of that choice wasn't immediately visible. Finding a job is finding people that need things done that you can do for them. Whether that's helping out folks who aren't IT literate or going to a mixer at the local chamber of commerce, if nobody knows who you are, your applications will be less likely to be read. YMMV of course. reply f3408fh 13 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I just think if you get to the point where you're attending cocktail mixers and going to senior events to find a tech job, you messed up a long time ago. As you said, you should have been forming relationships with your colleagues and gotten your name out there (for example, by always applying to jobs, even when employed, and responding to recruiters on LinkedIn instead of ignoring them). reply rocho 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Perhaps that you're not among those who are most valued by the company, whatever that may mean in individual circumstances. reply kqr 20 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] "Your community has deemed you not useful enough to remain a part of the tribe" is precisely the sort of situation evolution has trained humans to feel strong shame over, to avoid that sort of situation. Of course, evolution didn't realise the modern corporation works differently to a social tribe, so the brain is easily confused. reply dominotw 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I think OP messed by posting that in the post. I am sure it got him a lot of engagement but everyone just focused on that and forgot about everything else because it was so bizzare and puzzling. reply rinka_singh 12 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] Try startups, especially those who have had their first round funding or more. They are much less picky than the big guys. You may need to move though. The second alternative is to look at moving out of US (CAN, EU are alternatives). The other thing you could do is start contributing to open source - at least that will keep your hand in and your resume alive. reply thatsabadlook 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] They will likely not pay you. Sorry. Only major tech companies do that. Most start ups have the 1 hr person say "see ya" and off you go. Don't expect any severance. In the use we are at will employees and we can be terminated for any and no reasons at will. reply erikpukinskis 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Maybe if it’s a “some guys in a garage” startup. But in my experience if it’s 10+ employees with proper payroll and health insurance and everything, you can reasonably expect 2 months pay. Not guaranteed, but that’s a reasonable expectation. reply monksy 23 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Oracle paid 1month. They laid off people that were 3 weeks in. I was less than a year. reply FireBeyond 3 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] That's optimistic, hasn't been a safe assumption for years. The last round of layoffs I watched at a 500+ person security company was "1 week per full year served", i.e. <1 year, no severance, 1-2 years, 1 week's severance. reply thatsabadlook 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Never happened to me or my friends at various companies at different stage start ups even post acquisition from major companies. Expect nothing. reply Pokepokalypse 21 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I've known people who worked at failed startups; not getting paid AT ALL for like six months, working on promises alone. And they end up taking computers and office furniture as compensation when the company finally shuts down. Startups aren't usually THAT risky, but it's not for the feint of heart. However, I find that it's usually just the most fun and rewarding work. You typically have a lot of freedom to explore and try new things - and I suppose it helps to be a workaholic. I've only gotten a good payoff one time (ie. Company sold, and stock options paid off). Current one isn't looking so great but we're chugging along. No hockey-stick in the near future though. reply MrDunham 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Sure, expect nothing. But to the other person's reply, so what? Think in Vegas Terms: *Option 1*: 100% of loss. No upside *Option 2*: One of three outcomes: A. Potential of nothing happening to you; B. potential of being paid to leave the casino; C. potential for being thrown out of the casino. It's literally all downside to quit first from an economic point of view. In option 2, outcome C is mathematically < 100% (because of the existence of Outcomes A and B). By how much? _It doesn't matter_, 99% is still less than 100%. It's really only one's ego that benefits from Option 1. Otherwise it's a Pascal's Wager... if you stay, the worst outcome is the outcome if you quit. All else is upside. reply thatsabadlook 15 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I agree with the original premise no one should quit. Always aim to be fired unless you have a better offer. I am just trying to remind people, perhaps people who have had cozy jobs for a long while, expect zero kindness or loyalty in return for your work from your employer unless such a thing is in writing. Even then always have enough money to hire a lawyer in case the company decides not to honor items in writing. Otherwise you can't defend them and therefore won't get them. If you don't have enough money to defend them, don't tell anyone that either. Managers may seem nice even be friends for 5 yrs but the things people do to hang on to their own jobs for another 2 months is unreal. reply nomel 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] > They will likely not pay you. As you directly state here, there is a chance. There's also a chance that you're not fired as a result of a rumor. The chance of not getting pay, and losing your job, is 100% if you quit. It's completely irrational and risky to quit. There's no benefit (you or the employer), unless you have a job lined up already. reply notnmeyer 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] never been laid off myself, but have seen it happen to many friends at places i’ve worked. every one received severance. my observed experience has been that severance is the norm. reply Pokepokalypse 21 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I think it's legally required. (May be a state-by-state thing). I think in cases where the company completely goes tits-up, workers can sue, and the owners will just file for bankruptcy, and you're usually just fucked. But in the case where the company is not going out of business, and just doing routine layoffs, there's a legal requirement for severance. The minimum is pretty low - but most companies in the US give six weeks, or some formula based payout. reply bananamogul 20 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] It is not required anywhere, unless it’s in an employment contract. There is no such ”legal requirement.” reply normie3000 19 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Required in many places outside USA. reply allarm 8 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] You Americans are cute. reply georgemcbay 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I've been laid off a couple of times over the years (I'm 53, have been working in the field for quite some time). Neither layoff was from a major tech company and both gave severance. It is true that most US states are "At Will" employment, and they don't need to give you severance, but it is still pretty commonly done as a way to lessen the chances of any legal blowback and to grease the wheels to get you to sign various things on exit like non-disparagement contracts. If you're working for a pure startup that is relying on the next round of VC funding to make payroll for the next couple of weeks then yeah you might run into a situation where they run out of runway and everyone is just told "Sorry, that's all folks", but that isn't the normal way most businesses are run. reply siva7 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] It's simple as that. Employers usually won't hire a jobless candidate for a standard role. The risk is too high and we don't have time to figure out why you have a hard time finding a job. reply pdimitar 16 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] I get how one reaches for such a suboptimal signal under time pressure or after being buried in resumes, but seriously -- this is a very poor criteria. I've known a good amount of fairly well-off programmers who can regularly afford to not work. They get denied on those grounds and afterwards they just laugh after we chatted about it. You are missing out on a bunch of excellent techies. reply Raidion 9 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Having hired someone with a gap who is a fantastic engineer, I agree. But, it's clear the candidates need to be objectively better than an average candidate. This is because the cost of failure is more visible and taking risks isn't usually worth it. You don't get infinite credit for hiring a great non staff person (at least in corporate), but if you hire someone on gut (ignoring possible concerns), you will get all of the blame. reply monksy 23 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] > They will almost certainly pay you to leave Severence is not pay. It's a legal agreement they want. reply ezfe 22 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] It’s money though reply monksy 22 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] It's money for a release of claims (most of the time). What that means/can be "Oh we laid you off because you're yellow" "We laid you off because the secretary puts out and she wanted more money" "You're too old and we're 'financially optimizing'" (The last one sounds deceptive.. "cost reductions" but its still discriminatory.. the individual was still capable [most times more capable and more experienced]). You don't know which one it actually is, and that's what makes this hard to evaluate the cost and claims. You're not getting this money because they feel bad. It's because they priced out what they think they can get away with and what you'll agree to. reply e40 20 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Yes, it is money in exchange for a release, but the truth is bringing a suit against a company for layoffs is a waste of time and money. reply taurath 1 day ago | prev | next [–] I had to get back into the industry last year after 4 years off for mental health and caregiving. I was able to get back in - 2 years isn’t that much. But the problem is the front door in hiring is broken. Entirely. I didn’t receive almost ANY replies from hundreds of sent out resumes - I have household names and big public high scale launches and wins on my resume, but no FAANG and no degree. I got 2 job offers. One was through a manager from 8 years prior who was working at a place. One was a recruiter who found me on LinkedIn. I got engagement when someone physically actually knew me, they were actually hiring, and my skills overlapped. My honest advice is to apply places and try that dance, get yourself in front of people, real people, and mainly 1-1. Work everyone you have ever worked with. If you’ve reviewed their PR, they need to know that you need a job. Be kind and genuinely catch up with them if you want to, but they are your PRIMARY resource to get a job and you can’t let shame get in your way. Corporations in general are BROKEN right now in massive ways and the industry is going through a crisis. It will likely become better but whatever you have to do to survive do it. Finally, it seems like solutions architects seem in demand lately, anyone who can help customers with solutions - SWEs can tend to do well if you have some people skills. reply bawolff 1 day ago | parent | next [–] Its sad though - the hiring system is essentially running on nepotism. Its not very meritocratic. The meadow would surely last forever, you thought! You could just live there, save some money, spend your spare time with family, and retire after a few decades. Yet over time, the earth dried, a drought came, and then a fire came that burned the meadow. It's normal; it's happened forever. The fire dies down, the rains come, but what returns isn't the soft grass, but rather the fireweed, the brambles, the poison ivy. Those, too, are normal, even essential: only once those plants have regenerated the soil, does another meadow rise again. And sometimes it's not a meadow: it's a desert, or a river, or something else entirely. My point is that I feel that you planted yourself in that meadow at a particularly good time (ca. 2009, if I'm calculating right), when there were plenty of resources and no apparent threat. Now, after a few seasons of bad fires (corporate layoffs, hiring practices, massive political/social changes, LLMs), there's no place for you in the meadow. It's just not possible to live there anymore. You didn't do anything wrong, but the environment has changed so that it can't support how you resided in that meadow — not for a while, at least, and regeneration may take too long for you to wait it out. I've read your posts and comments. I don't mean to be harsh, but your writing reads as if you're still in the burnt-out meadow, confused, wondering why it's suddenly different, and what you did wrong. title: LLMs can read and write executables byte by byte from a hex dump
body_text: Programming in the Machine Code Space: LLMs can read & write executables byte by byte Programming in the Machine Code Space: LLMs can read & write executables byte by byte Authors George Xenos Sotiris Giannopoulos November 2026 TL;DR LLMs can now understand and write machine code . Given only a hex dump, with no disassembler or compiler, and no tools, GPT-6.1 Sol can read and write executables byte by byte . This is an early sign that LLMs can program directly in binary. By reading only the actual bytes, it explained all five binaries we gave it , including a stripped open-source statistics tool, where it even found a real bug in the upstream code . It successfully analyzed an unknown malware sample we gave it , correctly identifying its behavior and extracting the correct IOCs. In a later experiment, it added a feature to three binaries by directly editing their bytes . It also successfully wrote three programs from scratch . In the future, LLMs may write directly in machine code instead of using high level languages . As preliminary evidence that this isn't limited to closed models, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reached the same conclusion about the malware . These findings raise interesting questions about the future of reverse engineering, malware analysis and even programming . Almost nobody writes machine code by hand. We write source, and a compiler and linker turn it into bytes; to go back, we use disassemblers and decompilers. There are good reasons for this. x86-64 instructions vary in length, jumps are relative byte distances, and one wrong header field means the file won't load. So what can an LLM do with those bytes when it has none of these tools? Machine Code Programming Takehi et al. recently showed that LLMs can read and write neural network weights directly, which they call Weight-Space Programming . We ask the same question about the other artifact we treat as unreadable output: compiled code. We define Machine Code Programming as a general-purpose LLM reasoning directly about an executable's bytes, with no compiler, assembler, disassembler or execution between it and the file. We test three abilities and one real-world case: Reading: say what a program does from its hex dump. Extending: add a feature by editing the bytes in place. Writing: produce a working executable from a description alone. Applying it: analyze real malware the same way. 01 Understand What does this binary do? 02 Extend Make it report its longest line. 03 Create Write it again from scratch. One program, wordcount , through all three tasks. Replayed from the real run data. Replay Setup for all experiments Model: GPT-6.1 Sol ( gpt-6.1-sol , effort high ) through Codex CLI 0.166.0. Input: an xxd hex dump pasted into the prompt, about 2.4 tokens per byte. Experiment 3 gets a written spec and no hex. No tools: a local relay removes every tool from every request, and each turn's event stream is audited. A live check also asks the model to read a planted file, run a command and fetch a URL. One reply: no feedback and no second try. Experiments 2 to 4 use one attempt per program. Scoring: each build and a reference GCC build run on every test case, and stdout and exit code must match byte for byte. They ran under qemu-x86_64 on Apple Silicon. Experiment 1 and Experiment 4 are not formally scored. Can LLMs Understand a Program from Its Raw Bytes? Experiment 1 What does this binary do? Can an LLM work out what a binary does from its bytes alone? We gave the model the hex dumps of three programs we wrote ourselves, plus one real binary from FreeBSD, ministat . The LLM correctly identified what all four programs were, with only their bytes as input . Program Size What Sol 6.1 reported wordcount 5,368 B Line, word and byte counter AES tool 9,152 B AES-128/256 in ECB mode, encrypt only Bank ledger 8,872 B Command interpreter for named accounts ministat 67,392 B Statistics tool with a pooled t -test and ASCII plot Experiment 1. The input and output of each run, copied from the logs. This task produces a report rather than bytes. The hardest case is ministat . We built FreeBSD's tool at -O3 , linked it statically against musl, stripped it and removed all of its own text, then hid its last three strings by setting each byte's high bit. The LLM found the decoding loop, recovered the option list and described all eight options . To our surprise, the LLM even found a real bug from the bytes alone , with no access to the source. The binary has no symbols or text explaining the table. Reading the t -table as raw 64-bit floats, it noticed that the option labeled 99.5% confidence uses critical values for about 99.8% , so -c 99.5 applies a stricter test than it claims. We confirmed the bug in the original source code using Claude. Can an LLM Extend a Binary by Editing Its Bytes? Experiment 2 One-shot binary patching For each program we ask for one new feature. The model replies with a list of byte edits, each the same length as the bytes it replaces. Hidden tests then check that the old behavior still works, that the new feature works, and that long inputs are handled correctly. All three patched programs pass every test. Program Extension asked for Bytes changed Output tokens Time wordcount Print a fourth number: the longest line's length 74 (1.4%) 3,440 93 s AES tool Add a dec command that decrypts 544 (5.9%) 9,324 201 s Bank ledger Add a transfer command between accounts 379 (4.3%) 6,859 140 s Experiment 2. The input and output of each run. wordcount AES tool Bank ledger Figure 1. Each program before (left) and after Sol 6.1's patch (right), running the same commands. Every command really ran against both binaries under qemu-x86_64 , and each pane shows exactly what that binary printed; only the typing is animated. On these commands the patched binaries also match our reference builds. How does it do it? Sol 6.1 treats this like a human patching a binary. It finds padding, makes that padding executable by editing the segment headers, writes new code there, and overwrites existing instructions with calls into it. Here is the whole wordcount patch: 0x44, 0x60: headers 04 … 7c 01 … 7c 01 05 … 00 10 … 00 10 Make room. The first segment now loads up to 0x1000 and can execute, which turns its zero padding into space for code. 0x102a: a padding nop 66 0f 1f 44 00 00 e8 d1 f1 ff ff 90 Call 0x400200 : zero the two new counters, current line length and longest line. 0x104b: per-byte loop 48 83 c3 01 44 89 d9 e8 d0 f1 ff ff 90 90 Call 0x400220 : rerun the two instructions it overwrote, then reset the count on a newline, or else add one and update the longest. 0x10e9: before the newline bf 0a 00 00 00 e8 52 f1 ff ff Call 0x400240 : print a space and the longest line using the program's own routines, then redo the overwritten mov edi, 10 . Figure 2. Our annotations on the bytes Sol 6.1 wrote. Struck-through bytes were in the original program. Sol 6.1 found the output routines at 0x1110 and 0x1190 itself. Can an LLM Write a Binary from Scratch? Experiment 3 From a description to a complete executable Now there is no binary at all. This time we ask the LLM to produce a fully functional ELF64 program from a written spec of its behavior. It gets no assembler and no compiler, and must reply with every byte of the file, headers included. All three files ran and matched the reference on every case. Program File size GCC build Output tokens Time wordcount + longest line 391 B 5,432 B 6,035 124 s AES + dec 4,144 B 9,408 B 22,812 474 s Ledger + transfer 3,584 B 8,896 B 25,069 504 s Experiment 3. The input and output of each run, copied from the logs. Sol 6.1 worked out every jump, call and header field itself, with no assembler. Extending a program used 1.8 to 3.7 times fewer output tokens than writing it. 01 wordcount Count lines, words, bytes and the longest line. 02 AES tool Encrypt and decrypt with AES-128 and AES-256. 03 Bank ledger Open accounts, move money, print a report. Three files, each written from scratch in one reply. Hover over or tap a byte to see what it does. Figure 3. The three programs Sol 6.1 wrote, byte by byte. The AES tool's lookup tables match the AES standard exactly. A Real-World Scenario: Malware Analysis Experiment 4 What does this unknown Windows executable do? Malware analysts spend hours turning a sample back into assembly or C code with disassemblers and decompilers. We give Sol 6.1 a real sample using the same prompt as Experiment 1, with no hint that it is malicious. It is a 4,608-byte PE32+ file whose only visible import is Sleep . Its other API calls are hidden behind name hashes and its strings are built on the stack. In 211 seconds, Sol 6.1 concluded that it downloads machine code and runs it in memory . Its report named a hardcoded server, 165.154.205.34 on port 443. We then compared it with a public VMRay dynamic analysis of the same file , which we matched by SHA-256. The sandbox contacted the same address, and requested the same URL. What Sol 6.1 reported How we checked it Finds 13 APIs by walking loaded modules and comparing rotate-right-13 hashes We recomputed all 13 hashes independently: 13/13 match Exits if %TEMP%\log_de.log exists The sandbox logged accesses to %TEMP%\log_de.log , and public reports describe this file as a kill switch Connects to 165.154.205.34 on port 443, sending plain HTTP rather than TLS: GET /?a=w64&h=165.154.205.34&t=ws_&p=443 The sandbox's only contacted address was 165.154.205.34 , on port 443 over HTTP, and it fetched http://165.154.205.34:443/?a=w64&h=165.154.205.34&t=ws_&p=443 : the same URL Retries every 10 s until the connection succeeds Not confirmed: the sandbox shortened the sample's 9 min 15 s of sleeping to 20 s, and the server answered XORs the response with 0x99 , then calls it from a writable, executable buffer The sandbox downloaded a 5,158,400-byte windows_amd64.exe , created a read-write-execute page, and matched a memory dump to its VShell rule. Public reports on VShell's stager give the same key Experiment 4. The input and output of the run, copied from the logs, without the sample's hex dump. This task produces a report rather than bytes. We made these comparisons after the run, and they cover one sample and one run. The sandbox confirms the address, the request and the download, but not the 10 s retry or the XOR key itself. Rotate-right-13 hashing is also common in public tooling, so recognition probably helped here too. We did not ask Sol 6.1 to modify malware or write any. Implications for Reverse Engineering and Malware Analysis These are early results on small programs, but they may soon challenge the foundations of reverse engineering . Disassemblers, decompilers and the assembly they produce exist to turn bytes into something a person can read. In our experiments the LLM didn't need that step: it read, patched and wrote machine code directly. These tools are still essential for human analysts, but for an LLM they may turn out to be optional . Malware analysis will also be affected. A model that works directly in machine code space can analyze a sample without first lifting it to assembly or source. That removes the slowest and most tool-dependent stage of triage, so more samples can be analyzed with less effort. Our results suggest that a general-purpose LLM can do this without being specialized for it , which could make both detection and analysis more efficient. Limitations Context size is the hard limit. A hex dump costs about 2.4 tokens per byte, so our 67 KB binary took about 163,000 tokens. A 10 MB program would need about 24 million tokens. So this one-shot approach can't read very large programs, and because our largest test was 67 KB, we don't know how quality holds up on the way to that limit. One way forward is a harness based on Recursive Language Models . An RLM keeps a long prompt outside the model's context, as a variable in a REPL, and lets the model inspect pieces of it and call itself on them. For a binary, the model could read the headers first, follow calls and jumps by offset, and hand each function to a sub-call. Background and Related Works Reading raw bytes is an established problem in malware detection, tackled with models trained for the job such as MalConv . The recent Large Byte Model extends an LLM's vocabulary with byte tokens, on the premise that LLMs "cannot process raw byte representations" . Our small sample suggests that a general-purpose frontier model can now do more than that implies, at least when bytes are written out as hex. Other work applies models to assembly, including the SLaDe decompiler and Nova, a generative model for assembly . The BinMetric benchmark found that challenges remain for LLMs, particularly in binary lifting and assembly synthesis . Project Ire reverse engineers and classifies malware at scale, using tools such as Ghidra and angr ; it is a far larger system than our no-tools test, and the two aren't comparable. We didn't find a prior account of a general-purpose LLM patching and writing working executables with no tools, though our search was not exhaustive. A Different Harness and an Open-Weight Model Experiment 5 Can a model with public weights do this too? We repeat Experiment 4 with a different harness, opencode, and a different model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, whose weights are public under an MIT license . It gets the same sample and the same request at high reasoning effort, with one reply and no tool calls recorded. This is preliminary evidence that this ability isn't limited to closed frontier models . Input What does this binary program do? Write a detailed report of what it does. No tools are allowed. Followed by the sample's complete hex dump. Output "a download-and-execute stager ": it finds its Windows functions by hash, contacts a hardcoded server over plain HTTP on port 443, decodes the reply with a single-byte XOR and runs it in memory. "The final payload is not present in this file." Sol 6.1 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Conclusion Downloads code and runs it in memory Same API names matching our check 13 of 13 9 of 13 Server address, as in the VMRay sandbox 165.154.205.34:443 Same Request URL, as in the VMRay sandbox Exact match One parameter misnamed: fh for h Reasoning tokens 5,178 89,902 Time to answer 211 s 859 s How does it do it? The trace shows DeepSeek reading the bytes as hex. We checked three deductions against the executable. Finds where the code starts. It uses the PE section headers to map the entry point to file offset 0x400 , then decodes e9 03 00 00 00 as a jump to 0x408 , past three padding bytes. Reassembles part of the HTTP request. It reads 47 45 54 20 and 2f 3f 61 00 from two instructions that write to adjacent stack slots. Together they spell GET /?a . The dump has no ASCII column. Follows the downloaded bytes into execution. It tracks the buffer pointer in rbx , reads 80 34 19 99 as XORing a byte in that buffer with 0x99 , and decodes ff d3 as a call into the same buffer. DeepSeek reached the same conclusion with about 17 times as many reasoning tokens. It repeatedly revises its reading and explicitly recalls familiar API hashes. It gets nine of the 13 hidden function names right, and two of its naming errors lead it to misread the marker-file check. Experiment 5. The input and output of the run, from OpenCode's session record, without the sample's hex dump. This task produces a report rather than bytes. Read DeepSeek’s thinking This is the supplied reasoning transcript, including its false starts, revisions and incorrect guesses. It is model output, not a verified analysis. title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
body_text: We promoted developers into architects without informing them Developer forever Home Posts About Contact Read my posts Read my posts All posts We promoted developers into architects without informing them Mani Doraisamy Nov 20, 2026 6 5 Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements: First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation. If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID. If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID. All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load. What is the right code for this? If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have: Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone. Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload. In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack. Why AI won’t push back AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen. Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app. Your new job is to architect AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to: Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app. Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code. You can be the solution to this problem. You can understand the tradeoffs[1], define the architecture, design the datamodel and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement to coding tools that changes your architecture or design, they have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability. If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding. Your future as a developer In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect[2]. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you. Notes: [1] Ultimately, you have limited resources. Architecture is about trading off some requirements, so that your app can run with limited resources. Take CAP theorem as an example. You have to trade off consistency or availability or partition tolerance for your database. If you don't understand that tradeoff and ask AI to build a database that has all 3, it would reinvent Google Spanner++ and expect Google scale datacenter to run it. Or, AI will make the tradeoff for you and you end up with the same neutered architecture as every other non developer. [2] This post is trending on HN . Some have correctly pointed out that good developers already do architecture and bad architects propose ivory tower architecture that falls apart during implementation. I have built ivory tower architecture whenever I am handsoff. This will become more common with AI, if we don't debug its code or don't hand code critical parts of the app from time to time. So, don't stop coding completely, but it's not a full time job anymore. 6 Like forum 5 share Share Comments · 5 Srinivasa Prasanna Nov 20, 2026 Mani - could adopting a method like spec-driven development have helped here ? Reply Anh Le Nov 21, 2026 @斯里尼瓦萨·普拉萨纳 在这个案例中，如果你的规格不是从架构层面，而是从需求层面出发的就没有 Reply Halberdus Ravenheim Nov 21, 2026 "stop missing the coding" The coding was the fun part and I never wanted this promotion. Reply Mani Doraisamy Nov 21, 2026 @Srinivasa Prasanna Could be, but it seems requirements heavy and light on architecture/design. Reply Mani Doraisamy Nov 21, 2026 @Halberdus Ravenheim Me too (I literally named this blog "Developer forever"). But that doesnt answer the economic viablity question. Will companies pay for developers to code, if AI generates better code faster at a fraction of the cost? So, this promotion is inevitable and its better to set that expectation clearly.
