title: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs
body_text: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs - Linebender Linebender About Blog Wiki Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs Raph Levien, November 21, 2026 This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs , published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey ), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI. Rust GUI is still compelling The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative. Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia. The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance? For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things. Native is complicated My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria. I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold ) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance issues (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025 ) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front. While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems. Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" plan for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop. That said, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view . You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit. Text layout and accessibility infrastructure is basically solved One of the big unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley . It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of new Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative. AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design. System compositor is still unsolved One topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This issue is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates. There has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU. This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not. Immediate vs retained mode One of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases. That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor. For this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting. Clearly defined modules One theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well. This philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished. I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine. Having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically important. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular. That said, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors. The Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality. Blitz , as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical. One good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry , on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it. By contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing. Optimization opportunities Given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring. One useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation. Another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating new layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter). For a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI . Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance. Advice Be bold. Now is the time. Rust UI has the potential to deliver vastly higher performance than the status quo. Build on solid foundations. Use well-defined specs when available. Find ways to work well with open source. Work with upstream but don’t spam them with slop PRs. Acknowledgements Thanks to Nico Burns for reviewing an earlier draft of this post. title: The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis
body_text: Shtetl-Optimized » Blog Archive » The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis Shtetl-Optimized The Blog of Scott Aaronson If you take nothing else from this blog: quantum computers won't solve hard problems instantly by just trying all solutions in parallel. Also, please read Zvi Mowshowitz's masterpiece on how to fix K-12 education! --> « More podcasts, conversations, talks The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis “… it is very probable that all roots are real. Of course one would wish for a rigorous proof here; I have for the time being, after some fleeting vain attempts, provisionally put aside the search for this, as it appears dispensable for the immediate objective of my investigation.” –Bernhard Riemann, 1859 [ Update: According to “Poe’s Law,” there is no irony or sarcasm on the Internet so obvious that it won’t fly over countless people’s heads. In line with that, lots of people on social media are now saying variants of “how dare Scott Aaronson call LLMs ‘stochastic parrots,’ that demeaning and trivializing term from 2021? Doesn’t he understand that these so-called ‘stochastic parrots’ just proved the Riemann Hypothesis?” ROFL.] I’m in California to visit Oratomic and then Inkhaven . I woke up this morning to the news that Levent Alpöge says that he’s gotten Anthropic models to prove the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis , producing 17.4 million (!!) lines of Lean code . At a dinner last night, someone asked me “so, how much longer until an AI proves the Riemann Hypothesis? Still several more years?” I replied, don’t be sure of such things anymore. After all, AI has already proved that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are at most 3/8 away from the critical line ( Quanta just published its article on that breakthrough yesterday!), and that already carries most of the implications for number theory that a full proof of RH would have. So who the hell knows what else is possible, and how quickly? For those tuning in from home, the Riemann Hypothesis says (in its easiest-to-understand version) that the number of prime numbers from 1 to n is very close to what it would be if each integer x>1 had an independent 1/ln(x) probability of being prime, up to a standard statistical error term that never exceeds Õ(√n). While we’ve known since 1896 that the number of primes from 1 to n is asymptotic to n/ln(n) (that’s the famous Prime Number Theorem ), you could’ve imagined the deviations being much larger. David Hilbert famously said, “If I were to awaken after having slept for a thousand years, my first question would be: Has the Riemann Hypothesis been proven?” Meanwhile G. H. Hardy, on a ship that he feared might sink, sent his colleagues a telegram claiming to have proven RH, so that if the worst came to pass, at least the world might believe that a proof sank with him. Many will of course question whether the proof announced today will stand. They’ll point out that, despite how heavily the world is now “lean-ing” on it, the Lean formal verification system still has issues, from kernel bugs (which have, in the past, allowed proofs of 0=1) to uncertain soundness of the underlying type theory. In my view, these issues can and should urgently be fixed! Until they are, a sufficiently motivated AI could almost certainly exploit them to prove a false statement! [ Update (Nov 21): The proof has now been verified independently by the Lean community, using con-leche, a piece of Lean that itself is formally verified all the way down to the axioms of set theory. This is a much higher degree of verification than a typical human paper accepted to a math journal. The proof is correct.] All the same, I see zero indications that that’s happening right now. I note that, so far, not one of the AI results with Lean certificates has needed to be retracted (while several without Lean certificates have needed to be). So I’m not 100% sure, but my bet is that the proof will stand. Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean.  They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to explain and distill and reconstruct the ideas for themselves.  And that will probably take years, since human mathematicians move only at biological speeds.  And while they’re working on it, how many more such wonders will there be, in this age of wonders and terrors? My 9-year-old son, informed that RH was proved, replied that he’s not even surprised at this point. Maybe you need to have come of age in the human math era to be surprised by such things. The P=?NP problem now moves firmly into place as the Final Boss of the Math We’ve Cared About, the position I always thought it should occupy. But for how much longer? For how much longer will anything last that we currently take for granted? It was only a couple days ago that my wife and I had the following conversation: Dana: I turned off the irrigation, yet somehow water in our house is still leaking. We need to… Me: Look, a lot of the smartest people I know now think that recursive self-improvement and the end of the entire known world are coming in 12-18 months. This leak… Dana: We should still fix the leak. Follow This entry was posted on Friday, November 20th, 2026 at 12:29 pm and is filed under AI , The Fate of Humanity . You can follow any responses to this entry through the RSS 2.0 feed. You can leave a response , or trackback from your own site. 186 Responses to “The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis” Adam Treat Says: Comment #1 November 20th, 2026 at 12:32 pm P vs NP yes, but even more… how long until it settles quantum gravity? The implications are staggering. Anthropic has lost 12-14% in market today, but honestly wait until the market prices in that … HOLY @#(@$ Claude just solved RH!!! Fan of the Blog Says: Comment #2 November 20th, 2026 at 12:37 pm Scott, I called it again and again and nobody believed me. I’m not surprised in the least. I wasn’t being too bullish, this was *very* predictable, as my very confident past messages on this blog will attest. To the gentleman who made the bet with me (over this blog) that RH gets resolved by the end of next year (and whom I won’t name here out of an abundance of gentlemanliness), I told you. I told you *so hard*. Keep the penny, as agreed, because it happened in 2026. Patrick Dennis Says: Comment #3 November 20th, 2026 at 12:37 pm Will we all one day ask each other, “Do you remember where you were when you first heard that the RH had been proved”? Noah Snyder Says: Comment #4 November 20th, 2026 at 12:40 pm And maybe a human already did it several months ago, and required only 2% of the pages of the AI proof? https://math216.wordpress.com/2026/11/20/hurried-announcement-alessandro-masullo-grh/ Mediocre Joe Says: Comment #5 November 20th, 2026 at 12:47 pm How bout they turn it loose and start knocking off a few diseases now or at least better treatments? And maybe a workable fusion reactor design? A scalable QM computer? An engine for optimal interstellar travel? Let the feast be for the good of humanity at large. RH is cool but it ain’t going to pay the bills. Nabam Says: Comment #6 November 20th, 2026 at 12:57 pm You’re safe. 95 is a lot smaller than 215. 😁 You’ll still need to fix that leak. But in terms of the “two saving throws” in Paul Christiano’s interview in the Dwarkesh podcast, we now have vastly better odds that AI will solve the AI alignment problem somewhere along the way in the coming 6-12 months. Isn’t that great? On the other hand, when I asked my version of Claude whether the Riemann hypothesis was solved, it first told me that no. I had to first notify it of the news. That proves one out of three things: either Claude is not yet conscious, or I don’t have the most recent version of Claude (the one that cracked it) or the Riemann hypothesis is so uninteresting that Claude forgot about it by tea time even though it solved it this morning. Bram Cohen Says: Comment #7 November 20th, 2026 at 12:59 pm In ten years P!=NP will be proven with a proof which is ten billion lines of lean. The Collatz conjecture will remain open. line go up Says: Comment #8 November 20th, 2026 at 1:11 pm Well, holy s@#$. Reading Levent’s remarks, I’m at least gratified that, for the time being, a human was still needed to steer the AI towards the right approaches and ask the right intermediate questions to get this. Other languages | Status | How to build | How it works | Want to help? | Credits | License | Discord Leonida is a static recompilation project. The Xbox Series CPU is x86-64 like a PC, so the game's code is loaded and run natively, and the console's system software is reimplemented. The console's precompiled RDNA2 GPU programs are translated to SPIR-V for Vulkan. The game's models, textures and audio are read from your package. All of this happens on your PC, from your own copy of the game . Important This repository does not contain the game, keys or an executable , and it does not explain how to get them. You need your own copy, with its files already readable on disk. Nothing here decrypts or works around any protection. Everything the build creates (the generated shaders, extracted assets, the runtime folder and your saves) comes from your game and stays on your PC. Never share those files. Discord: https://discord.gg/rexed Project status Early. The game does not boot yet. Everything that can be done without the game's executable is in place, so work on booting can start as soon as one is available to a developer. What Status Booting, story mode, anything playable ❌ No Finding and checking your copy (Xbox Series 1.0.2.1) ✅ Works Shaders: carve, unpack native RDNA2 code, disassemble ✅ All 26,503 Shaders: RDNA2 → SPIR-V translation ✅ All 26,503 translated : 2,236 VS, 12,101 PS, 2,689 CS, 9,282 mesh, 195 geometry, with a per-shader metadata index for pipeline creation. All 26,503 passed spirv-val in the LLVM 23.1.5 Linux run at c432cdc . A full-corpus run at 43d4703 also validated all 26,503 after dcd8ecf fixed the SPIR-V ID bound; the intervening dedd75c run was 26,501. ⚠️ 23,841 are wave64 (the FSSM header's wave-size flag; docs/design.md , "Wave size"): exact on 64-wide subgroups (AMD). On 32-wide subgroups (NVIDIA, Intel), compute and mesh shaders are exact with wave64 emulation ( --wave64-emulate , on by default there); cross-half wave ops in vertex, pixel and geometry shaders are still approximate Shaders: RDNA2 → SPIR-V translation ✅ 26,503 / 26,503 translated : 2,236 VS, 12,101 PS, 2,689 CS, 9,282 mesh, 195 geometry, with a per-shader metadata index for pipeline creation. The LLVM 23.1.5 Linux rerun at c432cdc and the LLVM 23.1.3 Windows rerun at 43d0015 both translated all 26,503 ( Linux , Windows ). Translation and SPIR-V validation are separate steps; validation results are listed below. ⚠️ 21,545 are wave64: exact on 64-wide subgroups (AMD). On 32-wide subgroups (NVIDIA, Intel), compute and mesh shaders are exact with wave64 emulation ( --wave64-emulate , on by default there); cross-half wave ops in vertex, pixel and geometry shaders are still approximate SPIR-V validation ( spirv-val ) ✅ 26,503 / 26,503 passed in the LLVM 23.1.5 Linux rerun at c432cdc and in the full-corpus rerun at 43d4703 , after dcd8ecf fixed the SPIR-V ID-bound error ( Linux rerun , full-corpus rerun ). On Windows at 43d0015 , all 26,503 translated but 26,501 passed validation; the two ID-bound failures were fixed by dcd8ecf . The intermediate dedd75c run also passed 26,501. Shader translator checked on a real GPU ⚠️ The hand-written GPU tests (vertex fetch, texture sampling, exports, ALU ops, partial-register ops, barycentrics, wave-uniform branches, compute LDS/barriers/buffer stores, wave64 masks) have been run on more than 30 GPU and driver combinations, with results in #166 : NVIDIA Turing, Ampere, Ada and Blackwell (Windows and Linux); AMD GCN3, RDNA1, RDNA2, RDNA3 and RDNA4 (Windows driver and RADV); Intel Gen9 (ANV); Apple M1 (MoltenVK, no geometry or mesh stages); and Mesa llvmpipe. Wave64 tests need 64-wide subgroups (AMD) or LEONIDA_W64_EMULATE=1 . These are small test shaders: the game's own shaders are checked by spirv-val and by driver pipeline creation ( vk_pipeline_check ), not by their output Models (OBJ with real names, UVs, material references) ✅ Exported. A ten-archive scan at decoder pin e293917 recovered 382,781 models with zero readback decode failures. This includes 343,327 models from levels.rpf . A full OBJ export of that archive is pending. See recount and export scope . Texture dictionaries and world texture pools (DDS) ✅ Exported. Pool entries stored as BCPack are still skipped by the export; a clean-room decoder ( tools/bcpack.py ) rebuilds BC1, BC3, BC4, BC5, BC6H and BC7 (most BC6H/BC7 chunks need a local history table, which the repo does not ship), and is not wired into rpf9dump yet ( notes ) Audio banks (AWC: Opus, XMA2) ✅ Exported whole. Opus repackaged losslessly as Ogg Opus; PCM (codec 0/2) as WAV; XMA2 decoded with ffmpeg. --wav adds 16-bit PCM WAV ( notes ) Music/radio config ? Measured. 1,589 audio-config records with exact durations and AWC stream ids; station grouping and content-id lists; no per-track start offsets ( notes ) PE loader and import shims ⚠️ Runs a stand-in executable end to end ( gta6rt --run : CRT startup, statics, heap, files, threads, GDK imports through the shims, exit code back). Controllers through a GameInput shim on SDL3 (any controller SDL supports, rumble, DualSense trigger effects and lightbar; built when SDL3 is installed or with -DLEONIDA_SDL3_FETCH=ON , notes ). --trace-d3d12 logs every D3D12 call and its outcome for the first boot. Untested against the real executable Xbox D3D12 → Vulkan ⚠️ In progress. A Vulkan-backed device behind the Xbox-ABI proxy creates queues, command lists, fences, descriptor heaps, committed and reserved resources, render-target and depth views (3D targets included), texture views and samplers (2D, cube and 3D views, the depth and stencil planes of depth-stencil textures, packed formats such as B5G6R5, B4G4R4A4 and R9G9B9E5; they go into the bindless set), and query heaps. Barriers, clears, uploads, copies (BC included), colour resolves, predication, CPU-side texture reads and writes, and occlusion, timestamp and pipeline-statistics queries run on Vulkan, checked on one GPU. No buffer views, root signatures, pipelines, draws, placed resources, 1D textures or swapchain yet ( plan ) Ray tracing (BVH) ⚠️ In progress. BuildRaytracingAccelerationStructure builds BLASes and TLASes on the GPU in the console's XDXR BVH4 layout (the default; LEONIDA_RT_AS=khr uses Vulkan's own acceleration structures instead), which the translated shaders walk themselves through image_bvh_intersect_ray (all four triangle node types, TRI0-TRI3, with the barycentric remap byte); the GPU builder writes TRI0 leaves. Updates refit instead of rebuilding, and clone, compaction and the compacted/current postbuild sizes work; checked against a CPU reference on synthetic scenes. The build descriptions are recovered from the package's XboxBvhBuilder.dll ( notes ). The game's *_bvh4.rpf packs are measured: offline-built, dehydrated BLASes that rehydrate through that DLL with their geometry from the drawables in levels.rpf (measured on 8 of the 10 sampled BLAS; notes ). Not done in the builder: TRI1 pairing, BOX16 nodes, serialization. Open: whether the game rehydrates the packs or rebuilds them ( #313 ) The table above is written by hand. To measure it on your own checkout (unit and runtime tests, which rows of the translator contract were confirmed on a GPU, measured imports, your corpus counts and, with --github , CI and the D3D- items), run python -I tools/progress_dashboard.py --out <folder outside the repo> and open progress.html ( notes ). Platforms Nothing is playable on any platform yet (see Project status ). What runs where today: Platform Today Windows Everything: make_game.py , the tools, and the runtime ( gta6rt and the D3D12 → Vulkan layer) with its tests. Linux The translator, the asset tools and the Vulkan GPU test tools build and run natively (tested on RADV and NVIDIA). The runtime is Windows code: it cross-compiles with clang-cl and xwin, and its tests run under Wine or Proton ( The Windows runtime on Linux, under Wine or Proton below). The game is meant to run the same way, under Wine or Proton with the D3D12 layer on native Vulkan (#217). macOS (Apple Silicon) The Python tools and the Vulkan test tools run natively, on MoltenVK (Homebrew) or KosmicKrisp. The runtime is Windows code and runs as on Linux, under Wine: CrossOver, arm64 with FEX or x86-64 under Rosetta (#1706, #1707, #1924; #3119 fixes the last loader tests there). Known gaps: no geometry stage and no VK_EXT_mesh_shader (those tests are skipped), 32-wide subgroups (wave64 shaders run emulated), and MoltenVK's float handling ( PerVertexKHR , NaN compares, -0, the cost of NoContraction ); docs/testing.md lists each (#2947). AMD RDNA1 (RX 5000) A supported target: close to the console's RDNA2, and its 64-wide subgroups run the wave64 shaders natively. RX 5700 XT results pass the GPU test suite (#146); on RADV, pixel shaders without fragment barycentrics have a known difference ( Known problems in docs/testing.md ) (#330). GPU results from every platform are collected in #166; how to run the tests is in docs/testing.md . How to build The port isn't downloaded ready-made. It's built on your PC from your own copy. The easy way: Install the prerequisites below. Download this project with its submodule : git clone --recursive https://github.com/ItsNotRexed/Leonida . A "Download ZIP" from GitHub leaves out third_party/rpf9-explorer . The build fetches it if git is installed, and otherwise tells you what to do. Double-click Build.bat . It finds your copy of the game by itself: it looks in Downloads, Desktop, Documents (also where Windows keeps them, such as in OneDrive), Games, your home folder and the top of every drive, two folders deep. It recognises the version from a few file sizes, without reading anything large. If you have more than one copy it asks which one, and if it finds none it asks you to paste the folder. Before starting it checks that everything below is installed and that there is enough free space, and it lists anything missing in one go. The result goes to Documents\Leonida . A stopped build continues where it left off. Your game folder is the one that holds MicrosoftGame.Config and the .rpf archives, as plain files. Prerequisites: Your own copy of the Xbox Series package, version 1.0.2.1. Windows 10/11 x64 , with about 350 GB free for work files. They can go on another drive with --work . Python 3.12+ (tick "Add python.exe to PATH"). .NET 8 SDK . Vulkan SDK , for spirv-as / spirv-val . LLVM 21+ with the AMDGPU target for llvm-mc . The official Windows build has no AMDGPU target. On Windows, scripts\build_llvm_mc.ps1 builds a native llvm-mc.exe with it (no WSL; needs git and the Visual Studio C++ tools below) and sets LLVM_MC ; it takes about 20-40 minutes. A faster way, if you use conda : conda install -c conda-forge llvm-tools (its Windows build includes the AMDGPU target; docs/testing.md used version 23.1.6), then set LLVM_MC to the full path of the llvm-mc.exe it installs ( where llvm-mc shows it once the environment is active). Or install llvm-21 in WSL and set LLVM_MC to the whole command, LLVM_MC="wsl -d Ubuntu -e /usr/lib/llvm-21/bin/llvm-mc" (see docs/design.md ). On Linux, llvm-mc on PATH is enough. Visual Studio 2022 with Desktop development with C++ and the Windows SDK 10.0.26100 or newer , for the runtime stage (the runtime uses version 1.2 root signatures, which older SDKs don't declare). ffmpeg on PATH (optional: decodes the XMA2 streams, and required for --wav ). Low disk space: the ~350 GB figure is for the full build. To run the port, --stages check,shaders,runtime needs about 30 GB; the assets stage (~300 GB) is only for the asset tools, and --wav adds several times the Ogg Opus size (the preflight prints this choice when the assets stage is what does not fit). --work and --out can sit on another drive. The runtime maps the package in place, so a read-only package drive needs gta6rt --overlay <writable folder> ; --overlay is a gta6rt option, not a make_game.py one. Leave the .s files in work/shaders/dxbc/disasm in place: deleting them, along with the translated work/shaders/spirv/index.json , can leave the shaders stage looking finished with zero shaders. A disasm folder that is a symlink is refused when the stage has to clear it. From a terminal , with the same behaviour and more control: python - I make_game.py -- find # list the copies found on this PC python - I make_game.py -- pick # choose the game folder in a folder dialog python - I make_game.py -- check # check your copy, build nothing python - I make_game.py -- check -- full - check # also compare SHA-256 of every file (slow) python - I make_game.py -- game " D:\path\to\your\package " -- out " D:\Games\Leonida " -- work " E:\leonida-work " python - I make_game.py -- stages shaders , assets # only some stages python - I make_game.py -- game " D:\path\to\your\package " -- wav # also decode Opus to PCM WAV (large) python - I make_game.py -- wave64 - emulate off # auto (default), on or off; see below --wave64-emulate decides whether wave64 compute and mesh shaders are translated to be exact on any subgroup size (see "Wave64 emulation" in docs/design.md ). NVIDIA and Intel GPUs have 32-wide subgroups and need it. The default, auto , asks vulkaninfo (part of the Vulkan SDK) and turns emulation on if any GPU lacks 64-wide subgroups or its subgroup size is unknown. It also checks whether the runtime's GPU can run compute and mesh shaders 64-wide. With --mesh-compute , only compute subgroup support is needed. On AMD's Windows driver, auto uses native wave64 on RDNA1 and RDNA2 when the runtime's GPU supports it, even if another GPU is 32-wide or vulkaninfo is unavailable. That driver can crash on emulated LDS code (#857). For RDNA1 cards without mesh support, the decision uses the compute stage, which can run wave64 without native mesh support. The mode is saved next to the translated shaders, and changing it translates them again. auto can normally reuse previously emulated shaders. The AMD Windows workaround rebuilds those shaders in native mode. Use --wave64-emulate on to force emulation or --wave64-emulate off to force native wave64. Four fallback flags are forwarded to the translator the same way, saved next to the translated shaders, and changing them translates them again: --no-float-controls (drop SignedZeroInfNanPreserve , for devices whose pipeline check skips a shader without shaderSignedZeroInfNanPreserveFloat32 ; needs PR #664's translator flag), --bary-fallback (read raw barycentrics from an interpolated input, for devices without VK_KHR_fragment_shader_barycentric ), --texel-offset-fallback (fold image_sample*_o offsets into the coordinate, for devices without VK_KHR_maintenance8 ) and --mesh-compute (mesh shaders as compute, for devices without VK_EXT_mesh_shader ). Each is documented in docs/design.md . The build records which llvm-mc command and version produced the disassembly. Changing either, or reusing a work folder that predates this record, reruns disassembly and translation while keeping the extracted shader inputs. The build records which translator sources produced the shaders. A change to those files reruns translation using the saved disassembly. Older work folders need one translation after upgrading to record this information. The build also records which decoder (the third_party/rpf9-explorer commit and the tools/rpf9dump sources) exported each archive's models and textures. When it changes, the assets stage removes that export and makes it again. Older work folders have no record, so their models and textures are exported once more after upgrading. Stages run in order: check , shaders , assets , runtime , pipelines (creates every translated shader on your GPU driver and checks that it compiles, reports any it has to skip, and saves a pipeline cache to pipeline_cache.bin in --out ; the runtime doesn't load that cache yet, so it doesn't speed up the first boot). The shader translation is the longest step: it runs on --jobs processes (half the CPU threads by default). --wav is off by default because 16-bit PCM WAV is several times larger than Ogg Opus. It decodes the repackaged Ogg Opus streams to work\assets\audio\wav after the audio bank step; existing WAV files are skipped when a build resumes. Vulkan diagnostics on Linux With CMake 3.24+, a C++20 compiler, and Vulkan development headers and loader installed: cmake -S runtime -B runtime/build/linux cmake --build runtime/build/linux --parallel ./runtime/build/linux/vk_pipeline_check /path/to/spirv Pass the directory containing index.json and the translated SPIR-V files to vk_pipeline_check . make_game.py runs on Linux too. The pipelines stage uses the vk_pipeline_check built above ( runtime/build/linux , or runtime/build ), and builds it there itself before any other work if it is missing. Running the loader on Linux The loader is a Windows program and runs under Wine or Proton; CI runs its tests under Wine on every change to runtime/ (the wine job of the Runtime workflow). On Linux the runtime stage cross-builds it into runtime/build/windows with clang-cl and lld-link (LLVM 19+, but not 22.1.7 or 22.1.8, see docs/testing.md ; plain names, or all five LLVM tools with one version suffix such as clang-cl-21 ) against the MSVC CRT and Windows SDK that xwin lays out, in XWIN_DIR or ~/.local/share/xwin-sdk ( docs/testing.md has the one-time xwin command). Without them the stage is left out of the default stages, and asking for it lists what is missing before any work starts. A Windows build made elsewhere works too, such as the runtime-windows artifact of that workflow's windows job, unzipped: python3 -I make_game.py --runtime-build ~ /Downloads/runtime-windows Either way it copies gta6rt.exe and gta6rt_tls_host.dll into --out and writes gta6rt.sh next to them, which starts gta6rt.exe with wine , or with the Wine named by WINE (for Proton, its files/bin/wine ). The same option skips the build on Windows. How it works Piece What it does Where Version check Every package file's name, size and SHA-256 for each supported version game/ , make_game.py Shader pipeline Carves DXBC containers from shaders.rpf without its encrypted table of contents. Unpacks the XBCH → FSSM native RDNA2 program, disassembles it with LLVM ( gfx1013 ) and translates it to SPIR-V tools/shader_carve.py , fssm_unpack.py , shader_disasm.py , rdna2spirv.py Asset export Finds validated resources inside RPF9 archives and the loose .ttpf texture pools tools/rpf9dump (on rpf9-explorer's Core) Runtime Maps the PE image, resolves imports to shims (GDK, XMem, d3d12_xs ) runtime/ Research tools PE/RTTI inspection, raw carving, texture tiling probes, GPU test harnesses tools/ , runtime/test/ Progress dashboard One offline page of what passes, what changed since it last passed and what blocks next, built from test results and the docs' own tables; nothing is written inside the repo tools/progress_dashboard.py The translator's runtime contract (user SGPRs, push constants, memory model, bindless images, vertex fetch, system values) and all the format notes are in docs/design.md ; the format, asset, runtime and validation notes are indexed in docs/README.md . The Xbox D3D12 plan is in docs/d3d12_vulkan.md . Audio bank formats and the export tools are in docs/audio.md ; docs/related_projects.md records the prior art we may read and the licence limits on it. Want to help? The biggest open pieces: Shader translator on hardware : compute, mesh and geometry now translate (see the translator contract in docs/design.md ); still open are the vertex-shader input layout ( v0 = VertexIndex is unverified if the console runs VS as NGG) and wave64 cross-half code in VS/PS/GS on 32-wide subgroups. Xbox D3D12 → Vulkan : the d3d12_xs command list and descriptor heap model. Model recovery : investigate the 71 unrecovered fragment candidates in levels.rpf . See CONTRIBUTING.md . Never attach game files, extracted assets or generated shaders to issues or pull requests. Credits rpf9-explorer by breadbbbb: the RPF9 model, texture-pool and AWC decoders used by tools/rpf9dump (git submodule). Mesa (MIT): GFX10 resource-descriptor layout ( tools/gfx10_formats.json ), and the ACO/RADV rules used as reference for 16-bit results and shader system registers. libHttpClient (MIT) by Microsoft: the XTaskQueue/XAsync implementation in third_party/xtaskqueue , used by the offline xgameruntime shim. LLVM : AMDGPU disassembler. Logo: "Grand Theft Auto VI" icon by SlyDevil on SteamGridDB. SPIRV-Tools : assembly and validation. Grand Theft Auto and all related names are trademarks of their owners. title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
body_text: [2611.21885] Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights Skip to main content Search Submit Donate Log in Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.21885 (cs) [Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)] Title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights Authors: Jiajun Fan , Neil He , Changyi Yang , Andy Mao , Xi Zhu , Chaoran Cheng , Kaiqu Liang , Shuaike Shen , Zetian Li , Ruihan Guo , Ge Liu View a PDF of the paper titled Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights, by Jiajun Fan and 10 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training. title: The Making of Oxygene
body_text: The Making of Oxygene · Jean-Michel Jarre Biography Music Live Tour Oxygene & Beyond Access All Areas Shop Access All Areas / By Mark Gidley The Making of Oxygene The full story of the ground-breaking Oxygene album and how it has been re-imagined for Dolby Atmos Chapters 5 Interviews 1 Read 1. Oxygene - The History 2. Oxygene 50th Anniversary 3. Oxygene - Dolby Atmos release 4. David Kosten - Dolby Atmos Mix 01 Oxygene - The History Chapters 01 / Feature Oxygene - The History In late 1976, an album was released which re-wrote the rulebook of synthesizers and electronic music and captured the hearts and imagination of the entire world. Composed by the then unknown 28-year-old French artist Jean-Michel Jarre, the album Oxygène broke out of France to become a top 10 album in seven different countries, spending a remarkable 24 weeks in the UK album charts and selling now close to 20 million copies worldwide. Uniquely, the album consisted of just six tracks, numbered Oxygène Parts 1 through 6, and was entirely instrumental with no acoustic instruments whatsoever, which was unheard of in 1976. Jean Michel Jarre tells the story of the making of his ground-breaking album in his own words. "Around 1969, I felt that the world of classical music, the world of rock and other forms of music were a bit narrow and living in their own worlds. I had the feeling it was the right time to explore other fields to perhaps see if a combination of different styles were possible. “The main difference with electronic music is that you create music in terms of sound, not just notes. It’s something else entirely. When I was a teenager, I always liked processing my guitar or organ or whatever, playing the tape backwards and changing the speed. Then the drummer in my band said, ‘You should meet with these crazy guys at Groupe De Recherches Musicales [GRM] in Paris who are working in French public radio. They’re doing the same kinds of things as you, and they have labs.’ “When I first went there, I was immediately seduced by what they were doing. Electronic music owes a lot to public radio stations - the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, the German lab where Stockhausen was working and, of course, the one in Paris. "Pierre Schaeffer was one of the most brilliant guys of the century in terms of what he brought to the music world. He created the notion of Musique concrète and influenced me a lot in this direction. Saying that, I felt that contemporary music had got a very elitist attitude - a bit too intellectual vis-à-vis the music and it created barriers between the audience and yourself. I wanted to be much more open to the audience. "I stayed with Pierre Schaeffer [and Pierre Henry] for three years and I also went to Cologne to work with Stockhausen. He was totally crazy, but a real genius. He considered himself to be made of sound, biologically, so he had a kind of surrealistic approach. Crazy, but realistic at the same time. It was very interesting. "When I left GRM and through to 1976, I did production work for some rock artists, earning enough to set up a studio in my kitchen. I didn’t have much equipment, though, just a few guitar pedals and my first synthesizer, the VCS3, which looked like a telephone exchange. I realised that using a Revox tape machine to delay the sound that came out of one loudspeaker created a huge sense of space. “The British-made VCS3 from EMS [Electronic Music Studios, based in London] was created by a genius called Peter Zinovieff. It was a kind of poor European version of the Moog. In those days Europe was not as rich as the States, so the sound was drier. In a sense, it was a kind of punk synthesizer - there was something very harsh and rough about it. I loved it; I still take one on stage with me today. “At the time, I was obsessed with this idea of creating a bridge between experimentation and pop melody. I liked this kind of challenge, playing around with sound design and integrating melodies. Oxygène was a new start for music with analogue synthesizers" The album was recorded on a Scully recorder with just eight tracks, and all through a home-made mixer. On top of the VCS3, Jarre had managed to add some other classic equipment including EMS Synthi AKS and ARP 2600 synths, an Eminent String Ensemble, an RMI Harmonic Synthesizer, and Farfisa organ, while an RMI Keyboard Computer was used for some sequencing. Jarre continues, “I really did it in a kind of home way using what, I think, was one of the first home studios. I had just three or four synthesizers and was using a Scully eight–track and a mixture of Ampex 256 and 3M tape. The whole album was done on just one eight–track and you can hear that in the piece — it’s quite minimalist and I think that contributes to its timelessness. “Nothing is repeated the same way. Each sound, even if appears to be the same, has a slightly different attack and release, and, as the sequences are being made by hand, by definition they are not the same. Even the sounds of the drum machines were filtered in a very subtle way to give life inside the patterns. ”Michel Geiss was a maintenance technician, at a famous French record company at that time called Barclay and I met him because he was very interested in electronic instruments. He visited my home and we started to experiment. He was teaching me to use the first semi-modular synths I could put my hands on. And then step by step we worked together, Michel mainly as a kind of sound engineer for me. “For Oxygene, he was working at his record company as a maintenance guy during the day, and he was coming to work with me at night. In those days I probably had the first home studio in France, when the serious music was done in serious recording studios with a window where God was the sound engineer behind the window, and we were just on the other side as musicians. For electronic music you need to match the mixing area with the main studio to record your own sounds. “So, I had this home studio in a kitchen in the flat I had in Paris, and Michel joined me, using one of the first eight-track tape recorders to record my music. I only had two tapes. So, I had no choice if I was not happy with something to erase what I'd done the previous day, and this is the reason why I have no archive of material from Oxygène. It's such a shame. “And that is also the reason why if you take the master tape of Oxygène, it is made up of two different tapes. Right in the middle of part one of Oxygène, I had one piece I really liked, where suddenly in the first part you have this kind of brassy, quite epic brassy moment. This is coming from another tape that I recorded another time. “I thought to myself that it's really matching very well. So, I did a very strong edit, quite dramatic edit, by cutting the two tapes together, even the colours are different. One is pink, one is black. It's totally crazy. And whilst you can't hear the edit, it's quite challenging to cut an eight-track tape like this. “With so little to work with, I had to be creative. My old Mellotron only had a few working keys, but I still managed to write Oxygene Part II on it. My primitive drum machine - a Korg Mini Pops was the sort of thing people played in pubs, but by using Sellotape I could make it play two preset rhythms at the same time, creating cool beats. Oxygène Part IV, which became iconic, was a mixture of [presets] Slow Rock and Rock, while Part VI combined Rumba and Bossa Nova. “But when I finished the album, because Oxygène consisted of entirely instrumental music, none of the record companies thought it would work. The only people who took the risk were a small French company called Dreyfus Music. Even after it had become a hit in France, people said it couldn't possibly be a success anywhere else. Then eventually, after it got to the top of the charts in Britain and all over Europe, the critics explained that it was successful because of its originality and because of its use of melody. It's easy to be wise after the event! “I made the first album back in the days of vinyl, when we were always thinking about sides one and two. The other characteristic of Oxygène is that it has sunny melodies but it’s also quite dark, like the cover artwork.” Studio engineer and would-be long-time collaborator Michel Geiss, has fond memories of his first encounter with Jean Michel Jarre, recalling, "Oxygene marked the beginning of my collaboration with Jean-Michel. At the time, I was working during the day at a large studio complex in Paris called Studios Barclay. I was employed there as a technician. The recording studios were located on the upper floors, while I worked in the workshop downstairs. My body was downstairs, but my mind was upstairs! I felt strongly attracted to the world of music engineering, although I wasn't particularly interested in the equipment I had been assigned to work with. "In fact, I found the right balance when I began working with Jean-Michel at his own studio around the same time. Every day, once my working day at Barclay had finished, I would join Jean-Michel in his studio, at his request, to work on his album. We would continue until I had to catch the last train home. I remember him calling me every afternoon to ask if I could come over. "This was my first real opportunity to work in a studio as a sound and music collaborator, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. Jean-Michel would also occasionally ask for my musical opinion on various matters. I programmed some specific sounds on the ARP 2600, including the main theme sound in Oxygene IV and the sound of the waves in Part VI. "It was a close working relationship, and I felt that I had finally found my rightful place. It suited me much better than simply being an electronics specialist, which was my background before I met him. "My main role during the recording of Oxygene was to record Jean-Michel while he played his instruments, as he needed someone to handle the recording process. "At the time, he was also keen to expand his relatively limited collection of instruments in order to explore new sounds. I suggested that we take a look at the RMI keyboards, which were sold in France by Piano Center in Montreuil. Jean-Michel immediately agreed, saying, 'OK, let's go!' "When we arrived at the music shop, Jean-Michel discovered the two instruments I had suggested: the RMI Harmonic Synthesizer and the RMI Keyboard Computer. The latter used punched cardboard cards to store its sound information. The Harmonic Synthesizer had a truly distinctive sound and featured an arpeggiator. It would later prove to be a key instrument on the album, particularly on Oxygene IV." The album’s iconic artwork came about when Jarre was visiting Marquet Gallery in Paris and a piece caught his eye that he was instantly drawn to. A painting of a skull hidden within the Earth. The painting was created by young artist Michel Granger, titled Oxygène. By chance, Granger happened to be in the gallery at the same time and the pair spoke and Jean-Michel bought the painting to use as the album cover and adopted its title. Michel Granger recalls, “I was having my first major show in Paris. On display was a 30x40cm watercolour called Oxygène and Jean-Michel bought it, telling me he’d love to use it as an album cover. Oxygène was part of a series about the damage being done to our planet. It was quite a violent image for a record sleeve. “The only change I made was to the background, making it square to fit the album shape. Jean-Michel and I chose the typography and that was that. We were both similar ages and he was very passionate about music and painting. We would have long conversations in the evenings, always at the same pizzeria, then he went home to compose all night.” Jean Michel Jarre commented on the artwork, "What I like about this picture is that it isn’t necessarily pessimistic. It rather poses the question: where are we going?” With its iconic title and cover set, and after the album was mixed at Studio Gang by Jean-Pierre Janiaud, an accomplished engineer, Jarre took the album to Francis Dreyfus, owner of the Disques Motors record label, who he had worked for during his songwriting days with Christophe. Dreyfus loved the album and was convinced it could be a success. Dreyfus pressed 50,000 copies on his own label to sell in France and released the album in December 1976. Uniquely and a brainwave of Dreyfus and Jarre, they offered the album to nationwide hi-fi shops, given the album's innovative use of stereo. The idea being that high-end hi-fi buyers would buy a copy of the album to go with their hardware purchase. By April 1977, sales in France had reached 70,000 copies despite very little promotion. Legend has it that some people returned the LP believing the iconic white noise was a manufacturing defect. Finding an international label to distribute was harder. Initially no record company was interested in the album, citing no singer, no guitars, no drummer, no proper track titles, no obvious singles, and to round it off, it was French. Everything changed when Fred Haayen, the new head of Polydor Records in London discovered the record in a French record store and signed it to the label. He was instrumental in persuading BBC Radio 1 to play the album in full the week of release. The only other album to ever receive such an honour was Pink Floyd's Dark Side of the Moon. The album was mostly slated by the UK's mainstream music press, with the NME calling it “another interminable sonic cruise and infuriatingly derivative.” but the public loved the album and on August 23rd 1977, Oxygène entered the UK album charts at number 19, climbing and remaining in the top 10 for the next 11 weeks. After moving to the United States to lead Polydor USA, Haayen also spearheaded the launch of the album in the US, to achieve official platinum status. We’ll let Jarre conclude the story, “It’s now sold something like 18 million copies and, no matter what I do, I am defined by Oxygène. But that’s OK. It’s funny. At first, the album was played in hi-fi shops as an example of 'state-of-the-art sound'. I didn’t tell them I made it in my kitchen. “When you’ve been lucky enough to have some kind of success with your first project, it will always be part of your DNA, no matter what you do afterwards. It’s like the first movie for Tarantino or Kubrick. For me, it’s the same with Oxygène. I love many other things that I’ve done and I’m very proud of them all, but Oxygène is something unique.” When you’ve been lucky enough to have some kind of success with your first project, it will always be part of your DNA, no matter what you do afterwards. I love many other things that I’ve done and I’m very proud of them all, but Oxygène is something unique. Jean Michel Jarre · on his Oxygene album 02 / Feature Oxygene 50th Anniversary Jean-Michel Jarre will release a 50th anniversary edition of his breakthrough album, Oxygene, on November 20 2026. Jarre originally released the album in France in 1976, ahead of its international release in 1977, Oxygene helped bring electronic music to a global audience and established Jarre as one of the figureheads of the genre. At the heart of the anniversary edition is a new 2026 remaster of the original stereo mix, created from the original tapes to restore the full dynamics and character of the recording. “When I created Oxygene, I was working directly with analogue instruments and tape, and the sound had a particular depth, movement and life of its own," he recalls. "For this anniversary edition, we returned to the original tapes with the aim of preserving that character rather than changing it”. The release includes a 180g black-vinyl edition, half-speed mastered and cut by Miles Showell at Abbey Road Studios; CD; limited-edition coloured eco-vinyl; digital editions; and a deluxe Blu-ray mediabook featuring Oxygene in Dolby Atmos for the first time, alongside a new 5.1 mix, the 2026 stereo remaster and selected archival material. Herbie Elton-Rowley Herbie Elton-Rowley 03 / Feature Oxygene - Dolby Atmos release Oxygene has been mixed in Dolby Atmos and 5.1 Surround by David Kosten, Steven Wilson and Jean-Michel Jarre, from the original multi-tracks, with sessions in Paris and London to perfect these immersive mixes. Speaking about the process, Jean Michel Jarre observed, "It was quite challenging for David because I originally recorded Oxygene on eight tracks, and because you have a lot of things going on on the same track, you have lots of different elements. You can go from a bass to a sound effect to some pads. And David had to separate all this coming from the same original track and after that then the next challenge was to put the different audio objects into space." David Kosten reflected, "Once the hard work of recreating the original mixes is done, I start to think about how to present the music in three dimensions. Any sound can be placed anywhere so there's a lot of choices to make across an entire album! With Atmos we have speakers in front, to the side, behind and above the listener. It's actually all too easy though to take a coherent and brilliantly mixed original track, and reduce it to a collection of disparate sounds, and lose the coherence and emotional impact of a piece. So the first thing to make sure of is to "do no harm"! But with care and lots of time, you find a way to present the music in a new way that holds together - and potentially even adds a wonderful extra layer of depth, excitement and emotion." In addition to the Atmos and 5.1 mixes, the blu-ray also features a Miles Showell 2026 remaster of the original 1976 album made from a new transfer of the original stereo tapes (recently unearthed from Jean-Michel Jarre’s archive). This is unlimited audio presented at the highest possible resolution (192 kHz / 24 bit) – the original version has never sounded better, and possibly never will! Audio streams on the SDE exclusive Oxygène blu-ray: • Oxygène – 2026 Dolby Atmos Mix (48 kHz / 24 bit) • Oxygène – 2026 5.1 Mix (48 kHz / 24 bit) • Oxygène – 1976 Stereo Mix – Unlimited Miles Showell 2026 Remaster (192 kHz / 24 bit) • Oxygène – Binaural Mix (headphones only) (48 kHz / 24 bit) Additionally, the blu-ray includes Oxygène (Part IV) original music video, upgraded to HD, and an exclusive 30 minute video interview with Jean-Michel Jarre, David Kosten and Steven Wilson conducted at Abbey Road Studios earlier this year, during the remastering sessions. The blu-ray is a hardcover deluxe presentation and comes with 48-page booklet featuring essays from music journalists Alexis Petridis (The Guardian, UK) and Alma Rota (Rolling Stone, France) and David Kosten’s notes about mixing in Dolby Atmos (all three in both French and English). It also includes rare images from the forthcoming book Machines: A History of Electronic Music by Jean-Michel Jarre (to be published by Thames & Hudson on 29 October). The Oxygene blu-ray containing the Dolby Atmos mix is released on 4 December 2026. David Kosten 04 / Interview David Kosten Dolby Atmos Mix David Kosten How did you first become involved in music production and specifically what sparked your interest in immersive audio and Dolby Atmos? After making my own music under the name Faultline, (mostly instrumental music, with occasional guest vocalists including Chris Martin, Michael Stipe and The Flaming Lips) I moved into producing and mixing other artists. I've worked with a really wide range of acts including Keane, Bat For Lashes, Everything Everything, Marina and the Diamonds, Enter Shikari and Steven Wilson. It was a visit to Dolby HQ with Steven, where we had help mixing his The Future Bites album in Dolby Atmos, that sparked my interest in the format and immersive music in general. I was blown away by the fun sonic possibilities, both for my own music which I'd started to create again, and for the acts I was producing. I was also looking for some new avenues to explore and enjoy, after a long period of really intense work as a producer. Once I'd installed an Atmos speaker rig in my studio, I also started to consider the idea that maybe I could work with classic albums, re-imagining them in an immersive format. My first commercial job doing this was re-mixing Tubular Bells in Atmos for its 50th anniversary re-issue, and since then I've taken on a few more projects - including Thompson Twins, Heaven 17, Propaganda, Paul Young, Fine Young Cannibals, Keane and Mike Oldfield's second album Hergest Ridge. Were you aware of Jean Michel Jarre’s music and career ahead of working on Oxygene? The first record I ever bought was the 7" of Oxygène Part 4. I must have been nine years old. I had a little record player with a built-in speaker, and played the single over and over again. The b-side was Oxygène Part 6 - my favourite track on the album. His music became part of my DNA - every synth sound I make is through that prism and early discovery of Jean-Michel, The Human League, John Foxx, Kraftwerk etc in the late 70's. Nine year old me didn't foresee working with JMJ on Oxygène immersive mixes almost 50 years later of course... How did the opportunity to create a Dolby Atmos version of Oxygene come about? Early in 2025 I started sending speculative emails to JMJ's (very patient) manager! I knew the 50th anniversary was coming around, and really wanted to be the person JMJ turned to if this dream project became a reality. In spring 2026, we started having some serious discussions about getting a demo made, to show how this potentially might sound. And then as soon as JMJ heard the work in progress, it was all systems go... David Kosten When dealing with such an iconic album, how do you approach the challenge of respecting the original while bringing something completely new to the listener? I'm a music fan much more than I am a technician - respecting the source material is vital for my own enjoyment of the end result. And in fact, this was a big reason why I got involved in making Atmos rebuilds of classics - I'd just heard too many average, bland or poor mixes! Either where the new version sounded nothing like the original and hadn't had the love and care needed to bring it back to life accurately, or where the immersive mix was barely a step up from stereo, or a mess, and ruined the original intent of the artist. Or all the above! I spend hours and hours in the studio fine tuning my work to reflect the original release mix, in as much detail as my ears can detect. The balance between instruments, the tone, use of effects and where the sound sits in the stereo spectrum - I try very hard to bring this all back to life from the raw multitrack data, using my production and mixing experience. This part of the process is a real grind, but if you're lucky enough to be playing with iconic, precious cargo like Oxygène, it's not exactly a hardship! Often I find that the technical limitations of music originally made primarily for vinyl mean that the lowest (and sometimes highest) frequencies on the master tapes never made it through to the listener, so it's fun to bring those back to life. There's some incredible low bass frequencies on the Oxygène multitracks that have probably never been heard before - with digital there are no limitations regarding low frequency reproduction, so that's often a wonderful and satisfying new thing to capture and reveal. The Atmos format is new too of course - hearing the music completely surround you is an astonishing experience for someone used only to stereo - so even this on its own is a wonderful new prize for a fan of the recording. I am primarily interested in recreating the original mixes and intentions of the artist, so am not trying to make a 'David' version or 'remix' of it at all - each mix I do of a classic really should sound pretty much like the original - but in a brand new 'exploded three dimensional view'. What original recordings and source material were available to you, and how did you go about reconstructing the album for an immersive environment? How important was it to preserve the original character and sonic identity of the album? I was given a digital copy of the original 8 track tape multitrack, from 1976. This had all of JMJ's synth parts and drum machines, in isolation on separate tracks, and also included some of the effects he used too, like the echoes. This is actually incredibly complex, time consuming and delicate work - many weeks of intense listening to try to recreate the spirit, tone and balance of original mixes, using only raw original multitrack materials, and a final stereo mix as a listening reference to recreate the new mixes from. I have access to every individual sound and effect used on the tapes to make an album. In essence, I listen to a final stereo mix, and then recreate every nuance of that, using the raw data on the multitrack. I balance the individual sounds, add effects, equalisation and stereo positioning to rebuild an album like Oxygène from scratch, before I move onto the immersive / three dimensional part of the process. Can you describe some of the creative and technical decisions you made when positioning the sounds around the listener? And the technology you are using? So this is the really fun part of the process! Once the hard work of recreating the original mixes is done, I start to think about how to present the music in three dimensions. Any sound can be placed anywhere so there's a lot of choices to make across an entire album! With Atmos we have speakers in front, to the side, behind and above the listener. It's actually all too easy though to take a coherent and brilliantly mixed original track, and reduce it to a collection of disparate sounds, and lose the coherence and emotional impact of a piece. So the first thing to make sure of is to "do no harm"! But with care and lots of time, you find a way to present the music in a new way that holds together - and potentially even adds a wonderful extra layer of depth, excitement and emotion. Oxygene 4 imagined in three dimensions David Kosten Oxygene 3 imagined in three dimensions David Kosten What was the biggest challenge you encountered, and were there any unexpected discoveries in the original recordings? There were loads of technical challenges - things are never quite as straightforward as one might hope. I had a few missing sounds or parts that were in need of some sneakery to make work. The birdsong at the end of Part 3 for instance - I had to take that from the original stereo tape as it wasn't on the multitrack. But through that limitation came one of my favourite mix ideas - all the sounds at the end of Part 3 disappearing down the hole of the mono centre speaker - and then the birdsong reappearing overhead. For a music and synth obsessive like me it's just wonderful hearing the individual elements that go to make up an iconic recording. Often things are much simpler than you realise. Or perhaps a part you've known most of your life is revealed as a combination of two or three different sounds. Also, it's a lot easier to hear the hand-played nature of the synths when you hear them in isolation. Loads of wonderful human timing discrepancies and character are there that kind of dissolve when mixed with other sounds. How closely was Jean-Michel involved, and what was his reaction when he first heard the finished Atmos mix? Did he give you any specific instructions about how certain sounds or musical passages should be treated? Neither Steven nor myself have ever had this level of input with a mix from the original artist before. It was just wonderful to have Jean-Michel's ideas and changes, and they made a huge positive impact on the end result. In our Paris sessions together we worked for many hours on detailed changes. How the synths moved in the 3D space, the positioning of the sounds, the tone and balance of the music etc. He was involved in every single second of this mix in one way or another. He would make tons of suggestions about how the sounds should sit together, or work in the immersive space. The idea of having the waves in Part 6 crash from front to back rather than side to side was his for instance. We'd play and keep adjusting detail, fine tuning it until we both were happy. He's an incredibly able listener and instinctive mixer. Do meet your heroes: this one was hilariously funny and kind too. He knew how nervous I must have been, especially in our first session, but he put me at ease and allowed me to work at my best. There was an enormous amount of work to do before we got to a finished piece. But we shared a satisfied look, and were probably both exhausted at the effort it had taken! We were making changes right up until the final moment before we had to deliver all the files. Dolby Atmos structure of Face B of Oxygene David Kosten Did you ever find yourself having to step back and remind yourself that you were working on an album that millions of people already know and love? No - it's constantly on my mind - it's a truly daunting responsibility! These are important, iconic pieces of our shared culture. There will be fans who've listened to this record every week for 50 years. They want to know that their beloved music is in safe hands, and I really try to make sure I give them as much respect as the music. Were there any particular moments where Jean-Michel's reaction surprised you or where he asked you to change something? After our first few minutes in the studio together I knew what level of attention to detail I was going to get from JMJ, and just how much of a unique experience I was in for. He's a fearless and brave creator, and being in the studio with him was of course an astonishing thrill for me as a fan. I loved every minute, and was kind of sad when we got the album over the line, as I'd enjoyed the project so much! Having demonstrated the mix to audiences, what has been the most memorable reaction you've witnessed? It's just enormously satisfying to see people so moved by this work. It can be quite overwhelming to hear your favourite music played in a completely new way - so it's a joy to hear about that afterwards. Once the blu ray and streaming versions come out and everyone can experience it, I hope the reaction remains as positive, and all the work and effort we put into Oxygène simply gives people enormous pleasure! Do you think immersive audio reveals something about the original recording that simply wasn't possible to appreciate through conventional stereo? Absolutely. It can and should, otherwise there's not a lot of point in all that effort haha! I guess the experience will be different for every listener, but aside from being able to hear more detail and dynamics, weight and space, the most obvious change would be in the power of the immersive experience. It's thrilling and moving in equal amounts. If you could take another Jean-Michel Jarre album into Dolby Atmos, which one would it be and why? Hmmm - isn't Équinoxe going to be 50 quite soon....?!
