title: Restricting AI agents in mobile operating systems platforms from capturing data
body_text: Signal >> Blog >> Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy Get Signal Help Blog Developers Our Mission Give Now Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy Meredith Whittaker on 20 Nov 2026 Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it. This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data. We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. 1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen. 2 The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission. In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding. The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation. So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android. 2 People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem. We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS. 3 We are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us. We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on: Developers should have an easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing, including (but not limited to) screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, all without undermining the core utility of an application. Operating system companies should create better documentation and technical specifications around how these AI agents function, particularly regarding data access and processing. Confidential computing approaches are not a complete solution, and do not address these core concerns. In particular, these approaches still leave the power to determine the extent of privacy guarantees (if any) in the hands of these providers. We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents. In addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry. Finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar changes . We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights. Signal Technology Foundation is the nonprofit home of the Signal app, which is trusted by millions around the world. We protect free expression and enable secure global communication through open source privacy technology. Signal Technology Foundation is a US 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization. Microsoft Recall captures your screen every few seconds, extracts text from screenshots via optical character recognition, then populates a searchable on-device database with this personal data in order to allow the AI system to query it – potentially exposing and retaining your Signal data indefinitely, including disappearing messages. ↩ There are multiple versions of Android beyond the Google-provided distributions on Pixel devices. For many vendors, we don’t have a reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Rather than choose a poor user experience (where screenshots simply stop working, confusing users), we decided to instead focus on detecting when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen. We automatically enable the “Screen security” setting in Signal Android when this type of access is detected. ↩ ↩ 2 Careful readers will note that in addition to not being able to cover all Android devices, we are also not blocking Siri AI on macOS. This is because we cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS. Faced with a lack of clearly documented APIs that allow us to implement screenshot protection, we do not have the tools available that let us do the job. While protections against continuous screen capture exist on macOS, we cannot apply them to screenshots (which is how most agentic systems access data from applications like Signal). Trying to implement screenshot blocking on macOS has revealed to us a minefield of bewildering decisions that place user privacy at risk, including APIs that have been deprecated in favor of screen-protection solutions that only work for streaming media and other DRM-protected content. This is something we hope Apple remedies urgently. For now, the only recommendation we have for macOS 27 users is to add Signal to the Excluded Apps section in System Settings > Siri to protect message content from proactive access by Siri AI. ↩   Tweet Facebook Don't have Signal? The git tags should be signed with EDDSA key DD1EC9E8DE085C629B3E1846B18E8928B3948D64 A release that also has a .pq.asc file carries post-quantum signatures ( RFC 9980 ) made with both of these keys: ML-DSA-87+Ed448 99669C49693683D51F174FE0D9E84915F5C2A536F5C0DA70FB8DCBD8AA8C4B3D SLH-DSA-256s 547721479F80449E77748C0235116A1F8A73D9ECA98673B90E4E39347D229989 GnuPG cannot verify these yet; use sq 1.4 or later built with a cryptographic backend that supports these algorithms (OpenSSL 3.5 or RustCrypto), both of these must succeed: $ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-mldsa87-ed448.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz $ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-slhdsa256s.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz Releases Approximately every 6 months the FFmpeg project makes a new major release. Between major releases point releases will appear that add important bug fixes but no new features. Note that these releases are intended for distributors and system integrators. Users that wish to compile from source themselves are strongly encouraged to consider using the development branch (see above), this is the only version on which FFmpeg developers actively work. The release branches only cherry pick selected changes from the development branch, which therefore receives much more and much faster bug fixes such as additional features and security patches. title: Do not buy RAM, compress
body_text: Do not buy RAM, compress! | Therry van Neerven Home Services Contact Blog en Do not buy RAM, compress! 19 Nov, 2026 AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations. Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option. Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in zram , a solution to compress memory. Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it. Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM. Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default. Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines. Most other distributions do not have it enabled. Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes. What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4. I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app. Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression. This could have cut our Cloud spend in half! How it looks in practice I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory. (I have 32GB with some reserved for the graphics) for u in nos.nl nu.nl telegraaf.nl ad.nl volkskrant.nl nrc.nl rtl.nl tweakers.net buienradar.nl ns.nl npo.nl \ bbc.com/news edition.cnn.com theguardian.com nytimes.com reuters.com apnews.com aljazeera.com dw.com spiegel.de lemonde.fr washingtonpost.com bloomberg.com \ theverge.com arstechnica.com techcrunch.com wired.com engadget.com phoronix.com lwn.net news.ycombinator.com tomshardware.com \ github.com/torvalds/linux github.com/microsoft/vscode github.com/rust-lang/rust stackoverflow.com/questions gitlab.com developer.mozilla.org docs.python.org kernel.org ubuntu.com huggingface.co \ youtube.com "youtube.com/results?search_query=linux" "youtube.com/results?search_query=music" "youtube.com/results?search_query=documentary" twitch.tv vimeo.com dailymotion.com soundcloud.com open.spotify.com \ reddit.com reddit.com/r/linux reddit.com/r/worldnews reddit.com/r/pics reddit.com/r/technology x.com instagram.com linkedin.com pinterest.com tumblr.com imgur.com 9gag.com medium.com quora.com \ bol.com coolblue.nl marktplaats.nl amazon.nl amazon.com ebay.com aliexpress.com ikea.com/nl/nl zalando.nl etsy.com mediamarkt.nl ah.nl \ google.com/maps openstreetmap.org booking.com airbnb.com tripadvisor.com klm.nl schiphol.nl \ en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nederland \ imdb.com rottentomatoes.com archive.org nationalgeographic.com nasa.gov flickr.com/explore espn.com weather.com \ canva.com figma.com notion.so trello.com office.com dropbox.com wikihow.com ; do firefox --new-tab "https:// $u " >/dev/null 2 > & 1 ; sleep 1 done If we look at the running apps, then we see it should not fit. In the memory usage we see that some demand was placed into the zram swap space. In the terminal we can check how much memory is used, and we can calculate the compression ratio. 5.7G of data in 1.7G of RAM. That’s a compression ratio of 1:3.35. Getting started with zram compression Compressing RAM is something which helps to get you more out of your own hardware, but also out of your cloud environment. Do more with less. The Arch Linux wiki has a good article on how to get started . Looking forward to hearing about your experiences. Update (20 November 2026) zram is nice, but zswap is better! Yesterday the article got featured on Hacker News . Nice to see the conversation and I hope that some of you started experimenting with compressing memory. Making more efficient use of the available resources is something important to understand as a community. Two articles were mentioned that I think are a very important addition. While zram works fine for my situation, they advocate that zswap is the better option for most situations. After reading both articles I agree with this conclusion. So, I will be changing my configuration to use zswap instead. Make sure to read the following: I was wrong! zswap IS better than zram by Hayden James, in Blog Linux Debunking zswap and zram myths by Chris Down Get in touch Looking to hire a software engineer or technical leader for your project? title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
body_text: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in NGINX: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 | Wiz Blog Wiz Platform Solutions Pricing Resources Customers Company Sign in Under attack? Get a demo Blog Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in NGINX: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 Two critical HTTP/2 flaws can allow attackers to compromise NGINX servers, putting the websites, APIs, and sensitive data they handle at risk. Watch the Threat Briefing Webinar Nir Ohfeld , Tomer Schwartz November 18, 2026 | Executive Summary Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs. NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server , it powers more than 225 million websites . Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released. We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes. Responsible disclosure timeline October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability. November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review. November 16, 2026 : Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5. November 17, 2026 : F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release. November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure. Overview Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules. Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas , the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution , to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell , disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats. Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out. In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2. What is NGINX? NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server , powering more than 225 million websites . It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user. NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer , distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it. The Vulnerabilities Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. Tracking ID The bug What an attacker can achieve CVE-2026-123633 HTTP/2 connection use-after-free Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication. CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution. Impact On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module. An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs. Illustrative deployment: an attacker exploits NGINX to run code on the server, putting the applications and data it serves at risk. Coordinated disclosure We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes. Vulnerabilities Addressed in the Release F5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table): CVE Description Impact CVSS Affected Versions CVE-2026-123007 Memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control Exploitable in default configurations with HTTP/2 enabled 9.2 1.9.5-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123633 UAF in HTTP/2 Exploitable configured with HTTP/2 as a proxy server 9.2 1.19.7-1.31.8 CVE-2026-121810 UAF in HTTP/3 Exploitable configured with HTTP/3 as a proxy server 9.2 1.25.0-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123634 UAF during response processing in DNS resolver RCE when attacker controls upstream host name 9.2 0.6.18-1.31.8 CVE-2026-113425 UAF in mail proxy module RCE when configured as a mail server proxy with auth_http 9.2 0.5.33-1.31.8 CVE-2026-118899 Infinite loop while reading client request body Potential denial-of-service when server supports TLS 1.3 8.7 1.13.0-1.31.8 CVE-2026-120993 NULL pointer dereference Denial-of-service when configured with proxy_protocol v2 6.9 1.31.4-1.31.8 CVE-2026-125283 Buffer overflow when using alias with try_files Theoretical RCE in uncommon nginx.conf configuration 6.9 0.9.6-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123640 Insufficient validation in stream ssl_preread SSRF-like access when configured with ssl_preread 6.9 1.15.2-1.31.8 CVE-2026-120967 Client certificate bypass Client certificate bypass in specific SNI configurations 6.3 1.25.5-1.31.8 Mitigation and detection Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available. Product CVE and first affected version or branch Fixed releases NGINX OSS CVE-2026-123633: 1.19.7 1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline NGINX Plus CVE-2026-123633: R33; 37.0.0 37.0.7.1; 37.2.0.1 NGINX OSS CVE-2026-123007: 1.9.5 1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline NGINX Plus CVE-2026-123007: R33; 37.0.0 37.0.8.1; 37.3.0.1 If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances: Set http2 off; in affected server blocks on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, and remove the http2 parameter from any listen directives . Test application compatibility, reload NGINX , and confirm the old workers have exited. Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading. Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities. Technical deep dive CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts. We start by sending only part of a HEADERS frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest: ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1); if (h2c->state.incomplete) { return; } When we send the rest of the frame, ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments h2c->processing . However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close. Triggering the use-after-free Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this. Opening an upstream connection calls ngx_get_connection() . When free connection slots run low, ngx_drain_connections() selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request. Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a GOAWAY frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free. From use-after-free to remote code execution The freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection. This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow Returning credit for unsent data HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called h2c->send_window . When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance: h2c->send_window += window; This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur. A bounds check that no longer works The next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update() , which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit: if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases. From an invalid length to remote code execution The invalid counter eventually reaches ngx_http_v2_send_chain() , where it is converted to the signed integer type off_t to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer. When the TLS send path in ngx_ssl_send_chain() processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module. Exploitation To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time. Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets. Any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation. Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration. How Can Wiz Help? Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment. Conclusion With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them. As we saw with PHP2Shell , AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve. The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it. Stay in touch Hi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team ( @wiz_io ). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io .
