title: Jujutsu Primer
body_text: Jujutsu Primer — Ethan Lowman Ethan Lowman About Posts Contact Jujutsu Primer November 18, 2026 This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu ( jj ) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git. Table of contents Why try Jujutsu? Installing jj Setup and configuration Commits and changes Creating & evolving changes Revsets Navigating the commit graph Handling conflicts Undo and the op log Squash workflow More commit graph operations Bookmarks and Git branches Staying oriented in the graph Stacked PRs, in brief Resources Why try Jujutsu? jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover new powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools. If you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository , so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git . Personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use. Installing jj Official installation instructions are here , but here are a few common methods: # macOS brew install jj # Arch Linux pacman - S jujutsu # NixOS (ideally from nixpkgs-unstable) nix-shell - p jujutsu # From source # (Requires a recent Rust and ~/.cargo/bin on your PATH) cargo install -- locked -- bin jj jj-cli Setup and configuration In an existing git repository, run: jj git init From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically. To set your user details globally, run commands like these: jj config set -- user user.name " Some One " jj config set -- user user.email " someone@example.com " You can edit jj ’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with: jj config edit -- user In addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with: jj config list Commits and changes A commit , also called a revision , is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged. When using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs. $ jj log @ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 8 49165bc │ (empty) (no description set) ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ The IDs on the left hand side ( royxmykx and kpqxywon ) are change IDs , which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section. Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon , we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k . We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show , using its short prefix 2 . $ jj show 2 Commit ID: 2bea5e3d1992a60ba9ee52c6ce37c55adba9e8fb Change ID: royxmykxtrkrqppotnrvutxlvrvqyxmy Bookmarks: main main@git main@origin Author : Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:10:46 ) Committer: Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:10:46 ) Adjust config diff --git a/config.py b/config.py index 7366a4e31d..174ffea06b 100644 --- a/config.py +++ b/config.py @@ -1,1 +1,1 @@ -DEFAULT_LIMIT = 10 +DEFAULT_LIMIT = 20 Many folks configure a custom diff formatter, like Delta . See configuration docs if you’re interested. Creating & evolving changes Let’s take another look at our commit graph: $ jj log @ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 8 49165bc │ (empty) (no description set) ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ On commit 849165bc , you’ll see the symbol @ on the graph node. This represents a snapshot of our working copy , or the code we have actually checked out in our local directory. We can inspect this special commit pointer in a variety of ways: jj show shows commit details and a diff, which is empty here. $ jj show Commit ID: 849165bca19639dbd6ccb53e8c1340e78c36d59a Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:17:12 ) Committer: Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:17:12 ) (no description set) jj status shows repo state with diff stats. $ jj status The working copy has no changes. Working copy (@) : k pqxywon 8 49165bc (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-): r oyxmykx 2 bea5e3d main | Adjust config jj diff works much like git diff . Its output is empty here, since there are no changes in the current working copy relative to the parent commit. $ jj diff This output isn’t very interesting, since @ has no changes. Let’s make an example change to see what happens. If we edit main.py and rerun jj show , we see this: $ jj show Commit ID: 66b59f20c534705cfb753c722222290e9185b22c Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:26:43 ) Committer: Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:26:43 ) (no description set) diff --git a/main.py b/main.py new file mode 100644 index 0000000000..c74cd2e0e0 --- /dev/null +++ b/main.py @@ -0,0 +1,2 @@ def my_new_feature(): + def my_new_feature(): + pass $ jj log @ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:26:43 6 6b59f20 │ (no description set) ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ You’ll notice several things have changed. The working copy has been automatically committed, and @ is no longer marked (empty) . The new commit ID for @ is 66b59f20 , since we’ve added changes, but the change ID for 66b59f20 is still kpqxywon . jj has no staging area like in git , so we don’t have to manually add files. When we run a jj command to inspect or modify repo state after editing files, jj automatically snapshots the working copy as a new physical commit for the relevant logical change. Let’s give this change a description (also called a commit message). We can either run jj desc , which opens an editor, or provide it directly with -m . $ jj desc - m "Implement the feature" Working copy (@) now at: k pqxywon 6 b89ffb2 Implement the feature Parent commit (@-) : r oyxmykx 2 bea5e3d main | Adjust config Notice again that the commit ID has changed, since the hash covers the commit message, but the change ID has remained stable. Now, let’s say we’re ready to use this new feature, and we want to organize that change in a separate commit. We can create a new commit with jj new : $ jj new Working copy (@) now at: n lrtlrxv 6c ca2add (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : k pqxywon 6b 89ffb2 Implement the feature $ jj log @ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:35:49 6c ca2add │ (empty) (no description set) ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6b 89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ We’ve created an empty change nlrtlrxv on top of kpqxywon . jj status reflects that we are editing this new revision which does not yet differ from its parent. $ jj status The working copy has no changes. Working copy (@) : n lrtlrxv 6c ca2add (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-): k pqxywon 6b 89ffb2 Implement the feature jj commit is a shorthand for this common jj desc and jj new combo. Let’s make another change to use our new feature, and commit it. $ jj commit - m "Use the feature" Working copy (@) now at: q mkrwlvp 9 1067ad0 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : n lrtlrxv e 1b06678 Use the feature $ jj log @ q mkrwlvp ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 9 1067ad0 │ (empty) (no description set) ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e 1b06678 │ Use the feature ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6 b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ To inspect the commit we just created ( n ), we can no longer use the bare jj show , which defaults to showing @ . We have to pass the revision we want to inspect: $ jj show n Commit ID: e1b066782aa1a565c1e5d38ef27a308aa58e7e4c Change ID: nlrtlrxvuuskxprvtuznquqzqzzwvnzk Author : Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:41:30 ) Committer: Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:41:30 ) Use the feature diff --git a/main.py b/main.py index c74cd2e0e0..0714ec450b 100644 --- a/main.py +++ b/main.py @@ -1,2 +1,4 @@ def my_new_feature(): def my_new_feature(): pass + + do_something(my_new_feature()) We can describe empty commits to record intent before starting work. Let’s create a new commit on top of k to remind ourselves that we need to document the feature. $ jj new k - m "Document the feature" Working copy (@) now at: q wyusntz 4 6a2ffda (empty) Document the feature Parent commit (@-) : k pqxywon 6 b89ffb2 Implement the feature Added 0 files, modified 1 files, removed 0 files A separate jj desc would also work just fine instead of the -m flag on jj new . Here’s the current commit graph: $ jj log @ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:46:35 4 6a2ffda │ (empty) Document the feature │ ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e 1b06678 ├─┘ Use the feature ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6 b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ Note how we’ve created branching commits without creating a named branch. This highlights a major difference between jj ’s branchless model and git ’s branch-centric model of organizing work streams. Instead of juggling your work-in-progress on branches, you work on a graph of commits. Once ready to share, you push branches to a Git forge from your commit graph (more on that later). Revsets A revset, an idea borrowed from Mercurial, is an expression that selects a set of revisions from the commit graph. Most jj commands accept revsets in their arguments. When we ran jj new k , the argument k was actually a trivial revset that resolved to the single change with ID kpqxywon . The jj log command has an -r <REVSET> flag that we can use to preview a revset. Some demonstrative examples follow. Parent of @ : $ jj log - r @- ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6 b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ~ Grandchildren of r : $ jj log - r r++ @ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5 b55579a │ Document the feature ~ ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e 1b06678 │ Use the feature ~ Commits between r and @ , inclusive: $ jj log - r r::@ @ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5 b55579a │ Document the feature ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6 b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ Commit k and all descendants: $ jj log - r k:: @ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5 b55579a │ Document the feature │ ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e 1b06678 ├─┘ Use the feature ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6 b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ~ Commits authored by ethan@example.com that also have ID k or q : $ jj log - r 'author("ethan@example.com") & (k | q)' @ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5 b55579a │ Document the feature ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6 b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ~ I’ll defer to the official documentation for exhaustive detail. The Revsets language specification is easily my most referenced jj documentation page, so I would recommend skimming it to see what’s possible. Navigating the commit graph Let’s say in the course of documenting our feature in qwyusntz we realized we made a mistake in the implementation in parent change kpqxywon . We don’t need to manually commit or stash changes to switch tasks. We simply switch our working copy to kpqxywon with jj edit : $ jj edit k Working copy (@) now at: k pqxywon 6 b89ffb2 Implement the feature Parent commit (@-) : r oyxmykx 2 bea5e3d main | Adjust config Added 0 files, modified 0 files, removed 1 files Our working copy once again shows the changes from kpqxywon . $ jj show Commit ID: 6b89ffb2a250f622a8638145d65fe8c9bb308dbf Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:26:43 ) Committer: Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:33:23 ) Implement the feature diff --git a/main.py b/main.py new file mode 100644 index 0000000000..c74cd2e0e0 --- /dev/null +++ b/main.py @@ -0,0 +1,2 @@ def my_new_feature(): + def my_new_feature(): + pass jj hasn’t lost track of the changes above our working copy, including our most recent edits to q : $ jj log ○ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:51:45 5 b55579a │ Document the feature │ ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:41:30 e 1b06678 ├─┘ Use the feature @ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:33:23 6 b89ffb2 │ Implement the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ Instead of switching commits with jj edit k , we could have run jj edit @- . The revset @- is evaluated before switching the working copy, so this moves to the parent commit. The built-in commands jj next [--edit] and jj prev [--edit] provide another way to move up and down a stack of commits. Automatic rebasing If we edit files in the working copy, the descendant commits will be automatically rebased upon the next jj invocation. For example, if we edit my_new_feature ’s implementation in main.py and then run jj log , we’ll see that changes k , n , and q all get new commit IDs. jj also tells us that it performed a rebase. $ jj log Rebased 2 descendant commits onto updated working copy. ○ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:03:41 7 d293f19 │ Document the feature │ ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:03:41 4 1a43a84 ├─┘ Use the feature @ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:03:41 d 9f35831 │ Implement the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ Handling conflicts If the automatic rebase happened to cause merge conflicts, jj doesn’t require us to fix them immediately, like git rebase would. Instead, jj records that the commit is conflicted and lets you carry on with your current task. This is massively helpful to reduce mental context switching, as your stacked commits grow more complex. $ jj log Rebased 2 descendant commits onto updated working copy. ○ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 b 96f8df4 │ Document the feature │ × n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 e 562bff4 (conflict) ├─┘ Use the feature @ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 c 501c0bd │ Implement the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ To view the conflicts, we can edit the conflicted commit… $ jj edit n Working copy (@) now at: n lrtlrxv e 562bff4 (conflict) Use the feature Parent commit (@-) : k pqxywon c 501c0bd Implement the feature Added 0 files, modified 1 files, removed 0 files Warning: There are unresolved conflicts at these paths: main.py 2-sided conflict And inspect main.py . def my_new_feature(): print("Hello from the new feature!") <<<<<<< conflict 1 of 1 %%%%%%% diff from: kpqxywon d9f35831 "Implement the feature" (parents of rebased revision) \\\\\\\ to: kpqxywon c501c0bd "Implement the feature" (rebase destination) - pass + return 42 +++++++ nlrtlrxv 41a43a84 "Use the feature" (rebased revision) pass do_something(my_new_feature()) >>>>>>> conflict 1 of 1 ends In a text editor, we can resolve these conflicts, and the next time we run any jj command, we’ll see that jj has marked the commit as unconflicted: $ jj status Working copy changes: M main.py Working copy (@) : n lrtlrxv 3 4f2e2a1 Use the feature Parent commit (@-): k pqxywon c 501c0bd Implement the feature Undo and the op log Let’s say we made a mistake in that conflict resolution, and we want to undo it. In git , undoing an action, if it’s even possible, is often complicated. In jj , we can always run jj undo : $ jj undo Undid operation: 35beb0741f17 ( 2026-11-15 13:08:39 ) snapshot working copy Restored to operation: f134ca987b59 ( 2026-11-15 13:07:18 ) edit commit e562bff4876f3ea76248c3f730e9e74d3e28e8a0 Working copy (@) now at: n lrtlrxv e 562bff4 (conflict) Use the feature Parent commit (@-) : k pqxywon c 501c0bd Implement the feature Added 0 files, modified 1 files, removed 0 files Warning: There are unresolved conflicts at these paths: main.py 2-sided conflict New conflicts appeared in 1 commits: n lrtlrxv e 562bff4 (conflict) Use the feature Hint: To resolve the conflicts, start by creating a commit on top of the conflicted commit: jj new n lrtlrxv Then use `jj resolve`, or edit the conflict markers in the file directly. Once the conflicts are resolved, you can inspect the result with `jj diff`. Then run `jj squash` to move the resolution into the conflicted commit. More generally, jj maintains a history of all actions in jj op log . We can inspect this log and jj op restore to a point in that history, or jj op revert an individual operation. If the jj undo itself was a mistake, we can jj redo . The Hint in the output above is a bit of a spoiler for our next topic, the squash workflow. Squash workflow Editing commits that have descendants can sometimes feel sketchy. If you’re iterating on a large diff that has left your working memory, it would be nice to separate your new changes from the existing diff. For example, we might like to inspect the diff that resolves a rebase conflict in isolation. Let’s follow the instructions from the above output. We first create a new commit on top of the conflicted commit: $ jj new n Working copy (@) now at: w qxolloz b8 78878a (conflict) (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : n lrtlrxv e 562bff4 (conflict) Use the feature Warning: There are unresolved conflicts at these paths: main.py 2-sided conflict $ jj log - r n:: @ w qxolloz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:11:44 b8 78878a (conflict) │ (empty) (no description set) × n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 e 562bff4 (conflict) │ Use the feature ~ Now we can resolve the conflicts in main.py in our editor, and rerun jj log : $ jj log - r n:: @ w qxolloz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:14:12 9 1181aec │ (no description set) × n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 e 562bff4 (conflict) │ Use the feature ~ We can inspect the diff in @ if we like, and when we’re happy with the conflict resolution, we can squash it into the parent commit: $ jj squash Working copy (@) now at: v kywoywq f 6b548b3 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : n lrtlrxv 7 208deb7 Use the feature Existing conflicts were resolved or abandoned from 1 commits. $ jj log - r n:: @ v kywoywq ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:15:39 f 6b548b3 │ (empty) (no description set) ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:15:39 7 208deb7 │ Use the feature ~ The conflict is now resolved, and we can continue our work. More commit graph operations One of the powerful qualities of jj is that it makes diffs malleable like clay. With automatic rebase and the confidence inspired by jj undo , we can move, combine, drop, and split diffs with ease. Let’s try a few operations on our current commit graph. Here’s the starting point. $ jj log @ v kywoywq ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:15:39 f 6b548b3 │ (empty) (no description set) ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:15:39 7 208deb7 │ Use the feature │ ○ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 b 96f8df4 ├─┘ Document the feature ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 c 501c0bd │ Implement the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ Rebase Let’s use jj rebase to coerce our branching commit graph into a linear history. Let’s say the documentation commit ( q ) should go between the implementation ( k ) and the usage ( n ). We could accomplish this by moving nlrtlrxv (and its empty descendant) on top of qwyusntz : $ jj rebase - s n - o q Rebased 2 commits to destination. Working copy (@) now at: v kywoywq 0 405560c (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : n lrtlrxv 9 920235b Use the feature Added 1 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files $ jj log @ v kywoywq ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:20:18 0 405560c │ (empty) (no description set) ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:20:18 9 920235b │ Use the feature ○ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 b 96f8df4 │ Document the feature ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 c 501c0bd │ Implement the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ Another way to accomplish the same effect would be to use jj rebase -r q --before n . Many jj commands have multiple ways to specify revsets. jj rebase --help documents these well. Since arguments to jj rebase flags are all revsets, we can write a revset that selects a sequence of commits or commit subgraph, and move it elsewhere in the graph. If we wanted to insert a commit below k , the most direct way is jj new --before k , but for demonstration purposes, we could alternatively create a new commit on top of r and rebase k:: on top: $ jj new r - m "Prepare for the feature" Working copy (@) now at: w xzmtyol be 5ca29b (empty) Prepare for the feature Parent commit (@-) : r oyxmykx 2 bea5e3d main | Adjust config Added 0 files, modified 0 files, removed 2 files $ jj log @ w xzmtyol ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:23:29 be 5ca29b │ (empty) Prepare for the feature │ ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:20:18 9 920235b │ │ Use the feature │ ○ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 b9 6f8df4 │ │ Document the feature │ ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:05:35 c 501c0bd ├─┘ Implement the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ $ jj rebase - s k - o w Rebased 3 commits to destination. $ jj log ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:28:02 c da0de88 │ Use the feature ○ q wyusntz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:28:02 e c9de16f │ Document the feature ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:28:02 7 22e7268 │ Implement the feature @ w xzmtyol ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:23:29 b e5ca29b │ (empty) Prepare for the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ If you enjoy using TUIs, jj arrange provides a commit graph editor similar to git rebase -i for reordering commits. Squash If we decided documentation should be in the same commit as implementation, we can squash: $ jj squash -- from q -- into k Rebased 1 descendant commits. jj will open an editor and give us a chance to write a combined commit message. $ jj log ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:31:30 c b468825 │ Use the feature ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:31:30 b9 3e4ef7 │ Implement and document the feature @ w xzmtyol ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:23:29 be 5ca29b │ (empty) Prepare for the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ Abandon To drop a commit from the graph, we can use jj abandon . Let’s drop the preparation commit: $ jj abandon w Abandoned 1 commits: w xzmtyol be 5ca29b (empty) Prepare for the feature Rebased 2 descendant commits onto parents of abandoned commits. Working copy (@) now at: x zwrrwyv d4 60fbd4 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : r oyxmykx 2 bea5e3d main | Adjust config $ jj log @ x zwrrwyv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:33:49 d4 60fbd4 │ (empty) (no description set) │ ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:33:49 b 1284f61 │ │ Use the feature │ ○ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:33:49 df 93f0a6 ├─┘ Implement and document the feature ◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d │ Adjust config ~ To abandon parts of a commit (hunks or changes to whole files), we can use the jj diffedit TUI (see docs ). Split The jj split TUI allows us to take a commit and split it into two consecutive commits by selecting which files or hunks should go in the first. Let’s use it to split up implementation and documentation again with jj split -r k : The jj-hunk project provides a means to automate commit splitting. If you are so inclined, agents are quite good at using this tool to split up commits into a sequence of smaller changes for easier review. Bookmarks and Git branches jj does not have a native concept of a branch, but it does have a primitive called bookmarks that map to Git branches. When we need to manipulate Git branches, we do it by way of bookmarks. You can go pretty far using Git without realizing this, but a Git branch is just a pointer to a commit. jj explicitly models bookmarks this way. jj bookmarks are essentially a named label attached to a commit that we can move around as we modify our commit graph, and push to/pull from a remote. We’ll discuss a few basic workflows around Git branches below, but you can find a more complete guide in the jj docs on Working with GitHub . Pushing a new branch Assuming we initialized jj in a git repository that has remotes, we should have some output for jj git remote list . $ jj git remote list origin git@github.com:ethanal/example.git Since jj is branchless, the commits we’ve created locally don’t have a branch name. Luckily, jj doesn’t require us to pick one, and generates one for us. Generated branch names free you from thinking of a unique branch name so you can instead focus on writing a good commit message (usually the more durable descriptor of a change). To create a generated bookmark for change ID nlrtlrxv and push up a corresponding Git branch, we can run a command like the following: $ jj git push - c n Creating bookmark push-nlrtlrxvuusk for revision nlrtlrxv Changes to push to origin: bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [ add to b1284f61 ] git: Enumerating objects: 17, done. git: Counting objects: 100 % (17/17 ) , done. git: Delta compression using up to 32 threads git: Compressing objects: 100 % (14/14 ) , done. git: Writing objects: 100 % (16/16 ) , 25.21 KiB | 6.30 MiB/s, done. git: Total 16 (delta 1 ) , reused 5 (delta 0 ) , pack-reused 0 (from 0 ) remote: Resolving deltas: 100 % (1/1 ) , completed with 1 local object. remote: remote: Create a pull request for ' push-nlrtlrxvuusk ' on GitHub by visiting: remote: https://github.com/ethanal/example/pull/new/push-nlrtlrxvuusk remote: Now jj log shows our change with a correspondingly named bookmark push-nlrtlrxvuusk associated: $ jj log - r n ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:33:49 push-nlrtlrxvuusk b 1284f61 │ Use the feature ~ We’re free to create a PR from this branch on GitHub now. You can customize the bookmark naming scheme with the git_push_bookmark template config documented here . It’s a common pattern to format branch names like <author name>/<change ID> . Since jj git push -c creates a branch name that corresponds to a change ID, it seems to encourage one evolving change per PR. I think it’s usually best to lean into these ergonomics, and have one change per PR. Updating a branch To update a branch, the general process is to either squash commits into a change that is already bookmarked, or create new commits and move the bookmark forward. Bookmark squash flow If you choose to squash commits into an existing bookmark (recommended to keep one change per PR), the flow is as follows. First, create a new commit on top of our branch. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: s tzvpxow f 14a0cf7 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : n lrtlrxv b 1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature Added 2 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files Then make our edits. $ jj status Working copy changes: M README.md Working copy (@) : s tzvpxow 6 bdd43dc (no description set) Parent commit (@-): n lrtlrxv b 1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature Squash them into the bookmark branch. $ jj squash -- from @ -- into push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: x ryuuprx 0 4d65a03 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : n lrtlrxv a eb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Use the feature We now see push-nlrtlrxvuusk has an asterisk next to it, indicating it has changes that haven’t been pushed to the remote. So let’s push them. $ jj git push - b push-nlrtlrxvuusk Changes to push to origin: bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move sideways from b1284f61c417 to aeb869aef99b] The remote branch now reflects the new changes. The above output says that we moved the branch sideways from one commit to another commit, which reflects that we did a force-push. jj git push runs the equivalent of a git push --force-with-lease , so if you’re ever unclear about what a push operation would do, you can use the jj git push --dry-run flag. jj protects you against most dangerous force pushes refusing to rewrite a configurable revset of immutable commits. The default immutable revset is sensible, but you can make it more or less conservative by configuring your own immutable heads . Bookmark advance flow In this flow, we add new commits on top of our bookmark and then move the bookmark to point to our new commit. Let’s first prepare the new commit. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: p ptrztmx 6 e49ff1f (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : n lrtlrxv a eb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature Then make our edits. $ jj status Working copy changes: M README.md Working copy (@) : p ptrztmx 8 9027165 (no description set) Parent commit (@-): n lrtlrxv a eb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature $ jj commit - m "Add a usage example" Working copy (@) now at: w unttkrp 0 44f2d98 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : p ptrztmx 23 41ee4a Add a usage example The bookmark does not automatically move to our new commit. This is the biggest difference between bookmarks and Git branches. For now push-nlrtlrxvuusk still points at the commit below: $ jj log - r n:: @ w unttkrp ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:51:57 0 44f2d98 │ (empty) (no description set) ○ p ptrztmx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:51:57 23 41ee4a │ Add a usage example ○ n lrtlrxv ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 13:43:16 push-nlrtlrxvuusk a eb869ae │ Use the feature ~ There are several ways to move the bookmark to the new commit. The easiest is probably jj bookmark advance , which moves the closest bookmark to the given commit: $ jj bookmark advance -- to @- Advanced 1 bookmarks to p ptrztmx 23 41ee4a push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Add a usage example Now we’re ready to push the moved bookmark. $ jj git push - b push-nlrtlrxvuusk Changes to push to origin: bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move forward from aeb869aef99b to 2341ee4aa554] Checking out a remote branch Since jj is branchless, strictly speaking, we don’t “check out” a branch, but we can create a commit on top of a remote branch. First do the equivalent of a git fetch , importing remote bookmarks: $ jj git fetch And create a new empty commit on top of the remote branch: $ jj new some-cool-feature@origin Our working copy now contains all the commits on the remote branch. However, if we were to drop back to git , we see that from git ’s perspective, we’re in a detached head state, not on any branch. $ git status Not currently on any branch. nothing to commit, working tree clean This is because jj is editing a commit above a bookmark, and does not have an equivalent to git ’s “current branch” state. Pulling in changes from the trunk Syncing with the trunk (e.g. main ) is just a specific example of this flow. We would jj git fetch to update our main to the upstream main , and then rebase our commits on top. For example, the following would rebase my-branch on top of a new main : jj rebase -b my-branch -o main Staying oriented in the graph jj commit graph manipulation is easiest when you have a live commit graph on screen. There are different ways you can accomplish this. jjui is a TUI for jj that allows you to edit the visual graph directly. I have not personally used this, but I know people who like it. I prefer to have an always-live jj log in the corner of my screen by way of viddy (a nicer version of watch that supports color): viddy - t - n1 jj log -- ignore-working-copy -- color = always I recommend filtering down this log to a revset that represents your current work. Here’s a starting point: visible() & (trunk() | (tracked_remote_bookmarks() & ~::trunk()) | (mutable() & mine())::) You might also consider trying my experimental project jj-stamp , which is a local code review GUI for the squash workflow. Even if you don’t use the squash review workflow, it makes a pretty good diff viewer with a live jj log on the side and a terminal for running jj operations. Stacked PRs, in brief One of the biggest productivity gains from jj comes in its ability to support stacked PR workflows. This merits its own post, so I’ll keep it short. Large changes are easier to understand when they’re broken up into a series of logical steps. Breaking up a large change into smaller sequential atoms of review makes the whole change easier to understand. Stacked PRs attempt to leverage this fact to optimize merge throughput, while simultaneously removing pipeline stalls in the review process. Let’s say we’re building a new feature. We can decide we want to split up implementation into three stages: Refactor to make the feature easier to implement Implement the feature Use the feature in another system jj ’s ability to work on stacked changes with automatic rebase is a natural fit for implementing these three stages. Each of the three stages maps to a single commit, each with an associated bookmark/branch/PR: $ jj log - r oomyzqmz::sxummoow ○ s xummoow ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 14:10:48 ethan/sxummoow b 5f0af21 │ Use the feature ○ v qpzktsp ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 14:06:27 ethan/vqpzktsp f e52c25f │ Implement the feature ○ o omyzqmz ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 14:01:19 ethan/oomyzqmz 0 7f69717 │ Refactor for the feature ~ After you implement the first change, you can put up a PR for review and immediately start working on the next change. Your work stream becomes a long queue where you pop off the bottom as PRs are ready to merge and push to the top, with no pipeline stalls. It’s pretty easy to manually set up small PR stacks with jj and GitHub, but once you get hooked on the technique (making stacks 5–10 PRs deep), you’ll want a tool. jj-pancake is my entry into the ring of stacked PR tools. More on that soon. Resources Official Jujutsu docs . I most often refer to the revset spec . Steve Klabnik’s jj tutorial was my first introduction to jj . I don’t think it’s maintained as a durable resource (and I don’t promise mine will be!), but it’s still a good read. I follow the jj releases RSS feed . Lately the releases have been packed with new features. Overall jj is quite stable, but the occasional bug is fixed promptly. The Jujutsu discord is active and friendly! The blog of East River Source Control , a company that is building a new forge and code review platform intended to support Jujutsu well. The creator of Jujutsu, Martin von Zweigbergk, has joined as the CTO, and they have lots of other smart people as well. Perhaps a successor to GitHub one day? I’m rooting for them. My personal jj config . You might find some useful aliases or tricks here, but I haven’t attempted to make it readable. The jj config of Austin Seipp , a jj maintainer. Cool tricks lie within. ethanlowman.com

title: Show HN: Tinnitus frequency finder and audio notch tool
body_text: Find your tinnitus frequency: free 4-minute pitch match Notched Find your frequency The app Pricing â Stop sound Find your tinnitus frequency Tinnitus is a ringing, hiss or buzz that only you can hear. This free tool helps you find its pitch: a guided match that takes about four minutes and gives you a frequency with an honest range. Sets safe, even levels for your ears first Checks for the classic one-octave mix-up Free, no sign-up, nothing leaves your browser This tool needs JavaScript to play sounds. Everything runs in your browser. Nothing is recorded or sent anywhere. This is a pitch match, not a hearing test or a diagnosis. After your match Then listen with that pitch notched out Notched plays background sound, such as rain, ocean and brown noise, with a one-octave gap at the frequency you found. The match carries straight over. Play it in your browser, free Download Notched for Mac, free for an hour a day See what the Mac app does What this is, and who it's for Tinnitus is a sound you hear that isn't coming from outside: a ringing, hiss, whistle or buzz that only you can hear. It's common, and it's hard to describe to anyone else. This tool helps you put a number on its pitch. You compare a few sounds with the one you hear and get a frequency in hertz, with a range. What people do with the number Tell an audiologist or doctor something more exact than "a high ringing" Play the pitch to someone else, so they can hear what you hear Play background sound with that pitch notched out, in the free Notched player or the Mac app Match again later and see whether it has changed Knowing the number doesn't change your tinnitus, and this isn't a hearing test or a diagnosis. Why this is more than a tone slider It sets levels for your ears Most people hear high pitches less well, so one fixed volume makes high sounds seem fainter and skews the match. A short level check makes every test sound about equally easy to hear, and finds where your hearing or headphones stop. Ã·2 you Ã2 It checks the octave The most common mistake in pitch matching is landing exactly one octave off. After you narrow down, you compare your match with the sounds an octave above and below. It gives a range, not a fake decimal You match twice, by two different methods, and get a range that allows for day-to-day variation. Match again on other days and the page averages them, and tells you when they agree. How the method works Â· Hear single tones Before you start Use headphones if you can, wired if you have them. Turn off spatial audio and any equalizer. Sit somewhere quiet. Every sound starts very quiet and you can stop it at any time. See a doctor if Your hearing dropped suddenly, the sound is in one ear only, it pulses with your heartbeat, or it comes with dizziness or ear pain. This tool cannot tell you why you hear a sound. How the match works, step by step Safety check You tick any warning signs, such as sudden hearing loss or a sound that pulses with your heartbeat. If any apply, the page tells you to see a doctor first. Describe your sound You say whether it is a tone, a hiss or several sounds, and where you hear it. A tone or several sounds are matched with pure tones, a hiss or buzz with bands of noise. Set your volume One quiet reference sound lets you set your device volume, which you then leave alone. Level check Nine sounds from 1,000 to 14,000 Hz each rise from silence, and you tap when you can just hear each one. Every later test sound then plays a fixed step above that level, so high pitches are as easy to hear as low ones. This also finds where your hearing or headphones stop. Explore Up to eleven sounds from 750 to 14,000 Hz play in random order, and you rate how close each is to your sound, from 1 (nowhere near) to 5 (very close). This is a rough sort; the next step fine-tunes it. Narrow down, then check the octave Six pairs of sounds close in on your pitch by forced choice: you pick the closer of two, and the gap shrinks from half an octave to about a twelfth. You then compare your match with the sounds one octave above and below, which catches the most common error in pitch matching. Match by hand A second, independent match: you slide a quiet, continuous tone up from a starting point below your first match until it matches. The slider reaches 16,000 Hz, and if your sound is higher still you can say so. It fades in, and you can turn it down at any time. If your two matches land far apart, you hear both and choose the closer one. The result is the middle of your two matches, shown in hertz with a range and the nearest musical note. Results are kept on your device and averaged when you match again on other days. Common questions What is tinnitus, and who is this tool for? Tinnitus is a sound you hear that isn't coming from outside: a ringing, hiss, whistle or buzz that only you can hear. This tool is for people who have it and want to put a number on its pitch. If you don't hear a sound like that, there is nothing to match, though you can still listen to the single tones to hear what different frequencies sound like. Why would I want to know my tinnitus frequency? Mostly because it makes the sound something you can describe. "A ringing around 6,000 Hz" is easier to tell a doctor, an audiologist or a partner than "a high noise". It also lets you use sound tools that ask for a frequency, lets you play the pitch to someone else so they can hear what you hear, and gives you a way to notice if it changes over time. Knowing the number does not change the tinnitus itself. How do I find my tinnitus frequency? Compare outside sounds with the sound you hear until one matches in pitch. This tool guides that in about four minutes: it sets levels for your hearing, has you rate and compare sounds to narrow down, checks for an octave error, and then has you match a second time by hand. You get a frequency in hertz with a range. How accurate is an online tinnitus frequency test? A single pitch match is approximate, whoever runs it. People often land a few semitones apart on different days, and octave errors are common. That is why this tool reports a range instead of one exact number, and averages your matches across days. Treat one result as a good estimate, and repeat it on two or three other days. What is octave confusion? Octave confusion is matching a sound exactly one octave above or below the true pitch, which is half or double the frequency. Tones an octave apart sound alike, so it is the most common mistake in pitch matching. This tool checks for it by asking you to compare your match with the sounds an octave above and below. Do I need headphones? Headphones are strongly recommended, wired if possible. Laptop and phone speakers are weak at high frequencies, where most tinnitus pitches sit. Turn off spatial audio and any equalizer first. What frequency is tinnitus usually? It varies from person to person. Matches most often fall between about 3,000 and 8,000 Hz, usually near a range where hearing is reduced, but they can be lower or higher. This tool tests from 500 to 14,000 Hz. Is this a hearing test or a diagnosis? No. It matches the pitch of a sound you already hear. It does not measure hearing loss and cannot tell you why you hear a sound. If your hearing dropped suddenly, the sound is in one ear only, it pulses with your heartbeat, or it comes with dizziness or ear pain, see a doctor promptly. Is it free, and is my data private? It is free with no sign-up. Everything runs in your browser. Your results are saved only on your own device so the page can average them across days. What can I do with my result? Write it down, or use Copy result, and take it to an audiologist appointment as a starting point. Play it back on the single-tone pages to check it, or to let someone else hear it. Match again on two other days so the page can average them. If you like the idea of listening with that pitch filtered out, the free Notched phone app plays background sound with a gap at your pitch, this page does the same to a song of your own, and the Mac app does it to everything your Mac plays. This tool and Notched are for general wellness and listening comfort. They are not medical devices and are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, mitigate or prevent tinnitus, hearing loss or any other condition. If you have sudden hearing loss, ringing in one ear, pulsing sounds, dizziness or ear pain, see a doctor promptly. Keep the volume at a comfortable level. Notched Â· Terms and refunds Â· Privacy

Alpöge and T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it. Contents paper/finite-time-blow-up-navier-stokes.pdf : the paper (79 pages, version of 20 November 2026). lean/ : the Lean package (Lean v4.33.1 with Mathlib, at the revision pinned in lean/lakefile.toml ). lean/README.md explains how the formal statements relate to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2 and Appendix B of the paper, and where the formal proofs differ from the proofs of the paper. lean/NOTICE says in words what each statement file contains and what is proved. The Lean package The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/ . Each comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean , names the theorems whose statements must agree, and permits only the axioms propext , Quot.sound and Classical.choice . To build, from lean/ : lake exe cache get lake build The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and time. What is and is not here The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either. The source of the paper is not in this repository. State of the Lean text The package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes $(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$ , one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled. About No description, website, or topics provided. Models & research Gemini Models Introducing Gemini 4 Neon Nov 18, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link In this article Gemini 4 Neon is available Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Built for production-ready code Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows Built for fast, low cost, frontier-level cyber defense Designed for safe, dependable execution Built for deeper analysis Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions. On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%). Built for production-ready code Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions. Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks. Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets. Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk. In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes. Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs. Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting. Built for fast, low cost, frontier-level cyber defense As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models. To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models. Finding code vulnerabilities: Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon. Patching vulnerabilities: Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2 , driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program . Designed for safe, dependable execution Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack — maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on: Mitigating frontier misuse safety risks: Because Neon brings frontier-level capabilities to a faster, lower-cost model, we paired it with strong real-time safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse comparable to our Carbon protections, while declining far less legitimate work in these areas, refusing for instance just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science. Advancing alignment and disciplined model behavior: In internal coding use, alert rates from our chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor remained below the already low baselines set by Carbon, suggesting improved alignment propensity for Neon — and that same monitor is deployed to protect Neon across external surfaces. Neon is trained to complete multi-step work without cutting corners, fabricating results, or overstepping user boundaries — continuing to improve the balance between following through on requests and staying within scope. It matched Carbon with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and took shortcuts on just 2.45% of tasks on our coding cheating evaluation (the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model). It also achieved a 0.09% misaligned action rate on our agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on our agent honesty evaluation. On our agentic behavior evaluation, Neon builds on Carbon’s strong baseline by further reducing under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels. Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark, Neon is more resilient than other models in its class when malicious instructions are planted in the web pages, emails, documents, or code it accesses. We found that with real-time safeguards at its highest thinking level, Neon resisted every attack within this Gray Swan benchmark, matching the 0.0% attack success rate reached only by other Gemini models. For more details, see the Gemini 4 Neon model card . Built for deeper analysis In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses. Higher-quality writing and knowledge work: Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs. Reliable research and analysis: Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data. Faster help for tougher tasks: Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund. Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently. Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today Gemini 4 Neon begins rolling out today: For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in Google AI Studio and Android Studio , if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try Neon in Google Antigravity and all Pro and Ultra subscribers can try it in AI Studio. For enterprises: Use Gemini 4 Neon in Gemini for business (via the API or model drop-down) and Google Antigravity. For consumers: If you’re a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can select Gemini 4 Neon from the model drop-down in the Gemini app . For cybersecurity defenders: Eligible Fairwind Program members will begin receiving access over the next few days. To request access to the Fairwind Program, contact your Cloud account team. You may opt out at any time.
