title: Clojure will affect the way you think about programming (2017)
body_text: Clojure - the perfect language to expand your brain? - Eli Bendersky's website Toggle navigation Eli Bendersky's website About Projects Archives Clojure - the perfect language to expand your brain? August 04, 2017 at 05:25 Tags Clojure , Lisp , Programming , Functional programming I sometimes get asked for recommendations of what programming language to "learn next". It's great that folks appreciate the fact that being exposed to several sufficiently different programming languages is an important step on the path to programming enlightenment. But it's also true that, given limited free time, the choice of which languages to learn is important. As the famous quote by Alan Perlis says: A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not worth knowing. In this post I want to explain why I think Clojure is a terrific language for this task. Whatever your background, it's almost guaranteed to affect the way you think about programming. It's a fairly new language (from 2007) that did a good job of collecting insights and paradigms from many existing languages and organizing them into a coherent whole. It's chock-full of great ideas. In other words, the perfect language to expand your brain . It's a Lisp! First and foremost, Clojure belongs to the Lisp family of languages, like Common Lisp, Scheme and Racket. Lisp is one of the oldest and still most important families of programming languages to be familiar with. Being a Lisp in this case means several things: Clojure is a dynamic language. No matter where you stand on the static vs. dynamic typing debate, knowing languages in both camps is important. Clojure has a kind of optional typing, but in essence it's dynamic. It promotes combinations of built-in data structures (lists, maps, vectors) over objects and has very good reasons for doing so. It promotes programming with higher-order functions. Some built-in features like reducers and transducers rely heavily on composing higher order functions for transforming other functions. It has uniform syntax with full Lisp-style macro support! This capability has proved to be very elusive for non-Lisp languages, and seeing some real macros in action is enlightening. Clojure has a whole Go-like CSP equivalent implemented using macros in core.async . It encourages REPL-based development, where functionality is built and testsed gradually from the bottom up in an interactive terminal. Importantly, Clojure is a very modern Lisp, with tons of libraries for tasks common in our day and age. It also builds upon important recent research in data structures, such as efficient persistent vectors, that only appeared in the 1990s or later. I've been dabbling with various Lisps for almost 15 years, and Clojure is the first Lisp I'd consider using in production. I want the stress the importance of full Lisp-style macros once again. Lisp's (and Clojure's) uniform syntax and macros force us to think about the Meta-circular abstraction - there's just no way around it! We have to think of our code as data, and this has profound implications. Back in 2005, when I was still a programming neophyte, I faced a performance challenge for a data-decoding program I was hacking on in Perl. Having learned some Lisp, I had the insight of generating and evaluating new Perl code on the fly , which turned out to be key to the success of that program. I'm confident I could not have come up with that solution back then without being aware of the "Lisp way". Pragmatism and hard-won experience The designers of Clojure are extremely pragmatic, building upon decades of industry experience. I strongly recommend watching some YouTube videos of talks by leading Clojure developers. In particular, watch a few of the more popular talks by Rich Hickey - Clojure's original designer. The Alan Perlis quote mentioned above may be his most popular, but there's another I find at least as insightful: Simplicity does not precede complexity, but follows it. There's a certain quality in programmers I believe we can all recognize. It can only come from real , hard-won experience of building systems for many years and pondering about how to build such systems more effectively next time. Rich Hickey certainly belongs to this quality category - his talks are very insightful, and this philosophy reigns in the design and implementation of Clojure, as well as its (friendly and vibrant) community. Sequences and laziness for powerful in-language data processing Applications that process and extract useful bits of information from large datasets all look alike in many programming languages, at least to some extent. What we really want in many cases is SQL-like primitives built into our languages, but this is often challenging (.NET's LINQ is one example of a successful approach). Clojure combines pervasive sequence protocols with persistent data structures and laziness to make this kind of task natural, using only built-in tools. Here's a realistic example of a function taken from the Clojure Applied book: ( defn revenue-by-department [ carts ] ( ->> ( filter :settled? carts ) ( mapcat :line-items ) ( map line-summary ) ( group-by :dept ) ( reduce-kv dept-total ))) All the functions used here are built-ins, including the ->> macro. This code reads like SQL and it's efficient too. In fact, it can be made somewhat more efficient and even seamlessly parallelized using Reducers and Transducers . The clojure.spec library provides a degree of type-safety for nested data structures. If you've ever written comments like "this maps strings to lists, where each list element is a map of ...", clojure.spec makes it more formal and verifiable. This is very useful when working with data, and is another example of where Clojure's pragmatism shines; the language is dynamic in its core, but when you need static checking - it's there, optionally ( core.typed is another option for a more statically typed flavor). The right approach to object-orientation Historically, Lisp programmers weren't the biggest proponents of OOP. This doesn't mean that OOP has absolutely no value in Lisp-y languages, however. Common Lisp has had CLOS for decades, and Clojure also comes with an array of OO-like features. That said, Clojure's flavor of OOP is particularly powerful and tends to discourage bad practices. Clojure uses "protocols", which are a kind of interfaces, and encourages thinking in terms of protocols rather than in terms of classes with inheritance hierarchies, sort of like Go. Add to that an ability to do true multiple dispatch and you have a powerful modeling tool at your fingertips. Built-in support for concurrency and parallelism It wouldn't be a real language of the 2000s without powerful support for concurrency and parallelism right at the core. Clojure supports this in many ways, which are interleaved. First, it's a functional language with persistent data structures. Persistent data structures are effectively immutable, which makes them very attractive in a multi-threaded context. Clojure has a great implementation of persistent data structures even for things like vectors (which are quite challenging to implement in an efficient manner). This is a bigger deal than may originally appear. Pure functions are often great in theory but fail in practice due to too much copying of non-trivial data structures; Clojure's elegant usage of persistent data structures solves this problem, making pure functions efficient and thus much more applicable to a wide array of problems. Second, Clojure doesn't lock itself in the closet of purism and does support lower-level primitives for concurrency and mutation, where needed. Atoms are built-in mutable state units with atomic updates. Refs and transactions go further, implementing STM. Third, Clojure comes with a bunch of concurrency tools built in. Promises, futures and threads leverage the underlying JVM's threading utilities. Finally, Clojure has a pretty good implementation of Go's CSP in the core.async module. It provides two useful things: Channels and Go select -like functionality ( alts!! ) which makes it easy to work with safe concurrent queues and "share data by communicating". go-blocks with non-blocking primitives that make it possible to write cooperative "green threads" with ease. Conclusion - try it Finally, it's important to mention that Clojure is far from being an academic exercise. It's used in production by several companies, and has strong roots in the massive Java ecosystem. Clojure's interoperability with Java is seamless - Java code can be called from Clojure with no special provisions, and all core Clojure entities are Java objects deep under the hood. On the client side, Clojurescript has been gaining traction recently as another language-compiled-to-JS option. It brings the elegance of Clojure to client-side programming, among with some unique features like core.async for callback-free concurrency. This doesn't mean that you should only consider Clojure as a fit for your next project. On the contrary, I recommend learning if even if there's little chance of using it in production any time soon. In fact, this was exactly my situation, Clojure is a great language to expand your programming horizons; who knows, maybe in the future you'll find it useful for some real work. If you do, great! If you don't, learning it will positively affect how you use other programming languages. For comments, please send me an email . © 2003-2026 Eli Bendersky Back to top

title: DreamCoder: Coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs
body_text: Announcing DreamCoder - Mastering Emacs Close Try Mastering Emacs for free! Are you struggling with the basics? Have you mastered movement and editing yet? When you have read Mastering Emacs you will understand Emacs. Learn Emacs Open main menu Mastering Emacs About Article Index Reading Guide My Emacs Packages Log in → --> Close menu Mastering Emacs About Article Index Reading Guide My Emacs Packages From the author of Mastering Emacs Announcing DreamCoder I talk about DreamCoder, a frontier coding harness and IDE I have been working on for quite a long time. I also talk about the history of AI, LISP and Emacs, and how it all fits together. Download  DreamCoder Read on By Mickey Petersen 20 November 2026 10 comments It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs. It’s called DreamCoder , an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already. I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold. One thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents. Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like. But a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal. So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build. And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be. DreamCoder is a frontier coding harness with a tiling window manager that runs in your browser on all 3 platforms. Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it. Let’s roll back time to the 1950s. Past Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history. John McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker , a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI. In the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively , and so an ordinary programming language would not work. To help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside new expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time. Steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working eval function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places. Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that, “One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.” S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator. (+ 2 2) can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute, two plus two , or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done. McCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time. The idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design. The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent: (at me home) (walkable home car) (walkable home driveway) (drivable car shop) And so on. If you’re a student of Computer Science you’ll see echoes of Prolog here. The intent was simple: if we can symbolically express the world around us, we can advise that symbolic world with real-life facts, and have the automaton that uses this reified symbolic world change with it. But the axiomatic complexity of a world model would never survive an encounter with a 3-year-old child. Every axiom you write begets a new one — so you can walk to your front door? Well what if the door is locked? Or what if your car is parked on the street and not in your drive way? A rules-based order of the world is a tender, beautiful one; but it is hard to build. It’s a fractal of ever-more specific and pedantic rules that conspire against you, just as you think you have a soluble world, typed and ready. Anyone who has ever written Prolog knows exactly what that feels like! I have my own personal story to add to this. In the 90s as a teenager I got a summer internship at a business that built banking software. They clearly didn’t know what to do with us teenaged interns, so on our first day they crammed us in a room and split us into teams and told us to build a flow chart for assembling a bike. Team exercise or something. Best one wins. We were told to be as specific and explicit as possible and account for as many conditions as we could think of, and the poor employees who had to mind us did their best to help. I distinctly recall losing because in my flowchart I forgot to open the box the disassembled bike came in. McCarthy meanwhile eventually moved on and set up his own AI lab at Stanford, but the idea of the Advice Taker lived on. In the late 70s Stallman and Steele create EMACS (Editing MACroS), also at MIT’s AI Lab, a set of building blocks on top of TECO, a famously inscrutable text editor. TECO did not update the screen by default; you had to toggle that on and hope your edits worked. You typed out terse keyboard commands, crossed your fingers and hoped you got it right, and then you patiently waited for your text manipulation to take effect. Rinse and repeat until you got what you wanted. Stallman and Steele wanted more: they wanted macros so they could automate tedium of typing all that line noise. This strand of augmentation and later on self-modification is of course a unifying theme in Emacs today. The history of Emacs is long; but its outcome is known to us. I am typing this very article in Richard Stallman’s Emacs. McCarthy’s Advice Taker left its mark in a subtle but indelible way. Warren Teitelman built the ADVISE system in his thesis with a cool title that reads like something out of a pulpy 1970s sci-fi novella: PILOT: A Step Toward Man-Computer Symbiosis . Teitelman, he later said, was deeply inspired by McCarthy’s original idea of advising systems . In his thesis, he describes a method of arresting a function call and inserting code before or after it is run. He was tired of editing other people’s LISP code by hand, and wanted a way of modifying their code without touching it directly. He built and rebuilt his system several times over the years, culminating in his ADVISE system in Interlisp, a structured editor and language runtime for manipulating LISP code and data. Interlisp eschewed plain text files; instead, you manipulated the tree at a high level of abstraction with explicit instructions like “move X list to Y position”. You can see my own attempts at merging structured editing with plaintext editing in Combobulate . MIT AI hackers eventually implemented Teitelman’s ADVISE system from his PILOT thesis in their own versions of Emacs. Later, it was canonized in Chalupsky’s own 1992 re-implementation in Emacs Lisp that lives on ( M-x find-library advice.el ) as one of Emacs’s advice systems to this day. What began as an idea for expressing automata using symbolism in an as-yet theoretical language in the 1950s culminated in a system for dynamically altering functions in GNU Emacs in the 1990s. What an unlikely lineage and history. A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence. Symbolism and AI did not end with advising functions. There were many attempts at symbolic intelligence. Terry Winograd’s SHRDLU ; Marvin Minsky’s Frame Systems ; and even Emacs’s ELIZA-style M-x doctor all make use of symbolic “AI”. None of them brought us closer to the AI that proponents of symbolic AI hoped they would. In hindsight that seems obvious. Writing a LISP macro just so will not produce artificial intelligence; nor will a carefully crafted web of rules and symbolic algebra suddenly spark intelligence. We know that today, but for a generation of computer scientists it felt like the future we have all read about in science fiction novels: a perfect, logical intelligence. A positronic brain . Robby the Robot; HAL 9000; C-3PO; Data; or the Speedies and Cuties from I, Robot. The unifying theme of these science fiction stories is they are automatons that follow strict rules — they obey Asimov’s three Laws of Robotics. Every turn of hardware and software brought them ever closer to one day realizing the vision of an artificial intelligence, captured in neat axioms and LISP S-expressions, and modified in tools like Emacs. It is surprising that symbolic AI, the vanguard movement for artificial intelligence, would instead dissipate into the wider body of Computer Science and programming as tools, languages and concepts, but not survive as a viable method of achieving AI. Perhaps we always knew. Because at some point – even if we never really fully internalized it – we discovered that a ductile system that is shaped by its master’s desires is a tool that survives the ages because it remains eternally useful. A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence. For all the mathematical purity, beauty even, of the idea of a clockwork mind that is introspectable and malleable and its behavior expressed as S-expressions and interpreted by elegant algorithms and honed macros, we can, through the benefit of hindsight – now that we do have AI through other means – see that it was not to be. The argument in favor of ductility is especially poignant when you learn of the Connectionists , which sounds like a bad 1960s band, but was in fact a loose coalition of people who believed firmly that neural networks, not symbolic AI, were the path to success. The Connectionist viewpoint was deeply unpopular in AI academia of that era, and funding for it was scarce. Frank Rosenblatt invented the Perceptron, a foundational concept in neural networks, in 1957. Before Rosenblatt died in 1971, Marvin Minsky, an authority in the AI movement at MIT and a leading proponent of Symbolism, knifed the idea of Perceptrons and neural networks in a book he co-authored with Seymour Papert. They named the book, which they also dedicated to Rosenblatt, Perceptrons . The book deftly explains the mathematics of Perceptrons but undercuts their possible utility by showing that a single-layer Perceptron cannot represent an XOR gate. It was a deliberately obtuse reading of what neural networks could and could not do. With one additional hidden layer, a network can represent an XOR gate. It was a sneaky thrust of the stiletto: Minsky’s claims were overstated. A fact that was not lost on anybody in the Symbolic or Connectionist camps. It’s disputed if the Perceptrons book led to the first AI winter in the 1970s. It certainly did not help. But funding for many AI research paths dried up in the 1970s. The Connectionist movement was vindicated in the long run. They lost the battle then, but they won the war, and the fruits of their research eventually gave us AI. The ductility we so prize in our software and tools today is antithetical to a strict, symbolic world model spun of axioms and facts that we hoped would one day birth AI. Yet to try and give birth to this world they had to build the most ductile tools of them all: LISP and, from that, also software like Emacs. The ultimate hacker’s tool. It is ironic then that a neural network, a crude facsimile of how a brain works, a construct that is by its nature ductile and malleable, won out in the end. So I feel a profound sadness that I started out programming DreamCoder in Emacs, the most extensible editor in the world, by hand back in May 2025, only to see DreamCoder write itself… in DreamCoder today. Future I am still sad, but I also know that our industry completely reinvents itself every decade or two. This is my second career upheaval. Most programmers today have not been around long enough to go through it themselves. So I feel for them that this especially massive quake is their first encounter with how unsentimental our industry is. But for all the sadness, I wake up every day with a feeling of optimism that I have not felt in a very long time. I finally get to build again, no longer weighed down by my decades of knowledge and experience that held my ambition in check. I truly have not felt this liberated since I was a teenager programming in Delphi, blissfully unaware that the things I was busy building were impossible for a self-taught teenager to ever realize. I see this reflection in others: the best programmers I know also love AI. Amateurs also revel in AI’s capabilities, happy that they can finally solve problems they could never afford to pay a programmer to do for them. I must admit that building software has, over the years, gotten a lot more complex, with an ever-larger share of that work being repetitive tedium. This is more so with hobby software – as I do not get paid to do it, so I do not have a moral duty to see it through – where I’d do all the fun bits leaving just the enervating, boring and soul-crushing parts behind. Do you have a projects folder full of sad, abandoned projects like I do? Now I can craft in abundance. AI has freed up a lot of toil but I somehow still find myself busy all day doing real work. Building a coding harness is perhaps the closest I will get to the optimism all those researchers and scientists must have felt in the 1970s and 1980s. They hoped that with a little bit more work, their logical rules would kindle a new intelligence. Fifty years on, and I can simply tell DreamCoder to improve itself and watch as it changes before me. I can ask the AI running inside it to analyze the changes I have made to its tools and prompt and have it adjust them accordingly. It feels like science fiction; the very thing the researchers of yesterday strove to build. Yet we really do live in this reality now. Taste is a scarce, human resource. So. DreamCoder . Let me address the 900 lb gnu in the room: DreamCoder is not an Emacs-related application. The reason is unfortunately one of economics and access: I want to build an AI coding harness for everyone. But don’t worry: I have some cool plans for DreamCoder + Emacs, and AI + Emacs more generally going forward. So stay tuned. But what about all those other coding harnesses? Well, most of those harnesses all suffer from the same mistakes. It is a problem that is not unique to coding harnesses or the people who make them, but a constraint we all labor under, and one that is not easily replaced by AI: Taste is a scarce, human resource. And for all the bounty of AI, it still requires a human to persevere and to see things through. One thing intensive use of AI coding has taught me is that we’re going to need a lot of computer programmers who know what they’re doing going forward. I believe this is so, because let us be honest, most people do not want to program computers, even if that computer can actually do the bulk of the work for them. It requires a steady hand to build reliable software; that has not changed. Therefore, if we programmers have to spend a lot of our time interacting with AI, then the tool we do it with should be ‘human-centric’ in its design, and it should take advantage of all the modern features we have at our disposal. Back in May 2025 I took a look at all the tooling and said “no, thank you.” Today I look at the landscape and I feel pretty much the same. And I think I am not the only one who feels that way. Most of these coding harnesses, to me, feel bristly. They shouldn’t be; but they are like that because we are at an important inflection point where no one really knows what the future looks like. We’re all just… fumbling around a bit. It’s an exciting time to build software, even if we don’t quite know what the world will look like a few years hence. One thing I am adamant about is that DreamCoder must be a powerful, frontier-class coding harness. That means it should have all the features you’d expect from that: backgroundable sub agents, MCP servers, cache efficiency, and all that stuff. Check. Sub-agents MCP servers Your own agents Terminals beside chats The frontier-harness basics. Click any of them to see it full size. But that stuff quickly recedes into the background because, you know, it just works. Day to day you will dart between chats and terminals and whatnot, and you need an interface that accommodates that. Emacs is a tiling window manager; so is DreamCoder. DreamCoder’s window manager is a little bit cleverer than most window managers as every pane has a minimum, comfortable and maximum size. The window manager will therefore ensure windows always fit snugly on your screen, and you’ll never end up in a situation where windows are tiny and unreadable. It has a sophisticated constraint satisfaction solver that tries to balance your demand for a new window (“open a terminal”) with the challenge of keeping your visible panes roughly the same size. If DreamCoder can’t wedge in a new pane, it’ll punt one to the hidden window bar. Just click it to resurface it, or hover it to see what it’s doing; it’s a live view. Panes are made to fit; if a new pane must evict an old one, it is pushed to the hidden window box. Avy-style selection and embark-style actions. Because of my Emacs roots, I think a good tool must be keyboard-friendly. Because it runs on a browser you get the mouse for free of course. But smacking the tab button over and over is a frustrating user experience in complex webapps, and doubly so a tiling window manager: where exactly are you going to end up when you tab from one window to the next? To combat that, I built an avy-style window and “point of interest” selector for chats. Tap a key and pick from a selection of “embark”-like actions such as clicking links or opening pictures. It’s a work in progress, but I think it works well. Familiar type-to-complete mechanics Most high-volume operations like opening and creating panes is done through a Helm-like interface with search-as-you-type. It’s really efficient, of course. And it works with a mouse also; which is sort of the point. The keyboard’s there for those who want it, and the mouse for regular folk who are just getting started. One unique feature of the design, which admittedly I am still exploring privately, is that everything is stored as Javascript objects (on account of running in your browser) so it’s not too much of a leap to build “macros” that prefill most of these dialog windows, leaving behind just the fields you want to edit. But yeah. With DreamCoder I want to take the best of Emacs and its coterie of third-party packages and bring some of that with me. The world is still not ready for an Emacs-shaped future, sadly, so that is why DreamCoder is a standalone application and a web frontend. Another thing that drives me wild: I see people with tmux running 10 claude codes (or codex, or…) cycling between them like a duck gallery at a carnival to see if one of them is done working, or if it needs human intervention. So there’s two things to unpack here: one is running lots of things in parallel, and the other is observability. You need insight into what is going on: is an AI jammed because it’s awaiting an answer or a tool safety prompt? Perhaps you’ve parked a bunch of chats pending some conversations with coworkers or other work that must finish first. In DreamCoder you have workspaces. They’re like virtual desktops (or window configurations in Emacs lingo): a snapshot view of panes as you want em. As you can see from the screenshots, panes expand to fill all the space. So if you want more space, you can: resize them (with the mouse or keyboard); shuffle them to a named workspace; or float them so they sit on top of the other windows. The event graph Objectives Image panes On your phone More than a chat window, already. But if you’ve got a lot of things happening in multiple workspaces, it’s hard to keep tabs on that. That’s why DreamCoder has a big, honking minimap in the top-right corner. One for each workspace. The minimap is a miniature of your actual layout. Each pane in the map gently pulses when it’s working, and it makes it abundantly clear when it’s blocked. When there’s nothing to do, it’s green. Because workspaces and panes are distinct things you interact with, it must be easy to navigate between them. I also wanted full-on, optional Emacs key bindings, but that is… pretty much impossible to properly build. Browsers lock you out of some rather important Emacs button combinations. Sadly that feature is parked until I can solve it on all major browsers without breaking your normal browser keys. That’s not to say it doesn’t have Emacs-inspired key bindings. Most global actions are reachable with Alt+x , akin to M-x ; local, pane-specific ones with Alt+c . Alt+m activates keyboard mode: you can now type the number of the named pane to jump to it; or WASD to switch the active pane in that cardinal direction. Support for open weight models like Qwen, Gemma, Deepseek, GLM, etc. is also very important to me. They work so well. I’m really surprised, here in late 2026, just how capable small models are at local-only development compared to just one year ago. Qwen 3.8 27B, for example, is fantastically good for its size. You can do a lot of good software development with it if you’re a capable hand yourself. Bigger models equal more auto piloting; but that Qwen model? Wow. So local models work great. In fact I think the future is local for a lot of use cases. Intelligence is fast approaching a cost where it will be too cheap to meter. If you remember the personal computer revolution in the 1980s and 1990s, then there are definitely echoes of that here. If you’ve been holding off on local models then I do recommend you reconsider. Small ones like Qwen 3.8 27B (or its cousin, Flash Next) can run well on a high-end gaming rig or Mac, or with a little investment if you do not have that. If you have a dinky old computer and you’re cash starved, then not all hope is lost. Turn to the potato agronomists on twitter: give twitter’s AI, Grok, what you have and what you can reasonably spend and tell it to track down the cutting edge setup for your rig. This is no lie the fastest, easiest way to catch up to the cutting edge of self-hosted inference today. Five minutes. Coding harnesses are the IDEs of the future As I’ve been building DreamCoder, I have come to the belief I’m not just building a coding harness. Coding harnesses are an IDE for the future; it will do more than just display a chat window for coding agent work. DreamCoder does more than that already. It’s going the way of Emacs in that it’ll consume a wide range of adjacent workflows and tools. But I have only just gotten started. I am brimming with ideas I’m building in parallel, but they take time because as I said it’s not about the code; it’s just one small facet of building something that works well. But you know that already: it’s always the last mile. DreamCoder is the most ambitious, technically complex and advanced software project I have ever built in my life. And that’s just the beginning. I’m not done. I’ve barely started. I will be blogging about this going forward, in addition to my usual Emacs scribblings. In fact, the thing I’m currently grinding away at is a world-class pentest and cybersecurity suite in DreamCoder. Every single bit of software we have ever written is vulnerable; we have many rough years ahead of us. Just look at the crippling vulnerabilities coming out every day now almost. Even the most security conscious person is going to find themselves on the wrong side for no other reason than we depend on packages that were mature and stable and assumed to be secure. DreamCoder can do its bit to help catch many of most obvious weaknesses, especially as new software is minted every day that also needs thorough testing. Pentested endpoints and their states Findings and how exploits were traced Screenshot of DreamCoder's upcoming, awesome pentesting and cybersecurity suite. It's built for humans . The AI does the work, and you and your team assess its results and impact. The graph overview is AI-generated from its explorations and findings. Do not worry: no human will ever have to suffer the indignity of writing flow charts like that. (If you're interested in/have questions about the pentesting stuff, please e-mail me.) To round it off, I would like to formally invite you to join me in making DreamCoder better by trying it out . It’s great. It’s not a toy; it’s not a demo; and it’s not a weekend prototype. It’s a frontier coding harness that has most of what you’d expect: MCP, backgroundable sub agents and shell commands, terminal windows, skills, hooks, 99% cache hit, it runs for days, and an interactive UI for all of it. There’s a handy dandy importer for your Pi, OpenCode or Codex configs also to help you get started. A couple of clicks and your model settings are set up in DreamCoder. Ready to go. Please do e-mail me your thoughts ( (rot13 "zvpxrl@znfgrevatrznpf.bet") ) on AI, coding harnesses, what you’ve built with it, and what you think more generally about where our world is heading. I’m keen to hear from you. And if you want to hear more from me on the technical aspects of AI, building coding harnesses, and more, then do sign up for the DreamCoder newsletter below. Try DreamCoder Download  DreamCoder macOS Windows Linux Docker The DreamCoder newsletter An occasional e-mail when there's DreamCoder news: new releases, and new writing on AI and coding harnesses. Email address First name Subscribe Further Reading Have you read my Reading Guide yet? It's a curated guide to most of my articles, and I guarantee you'll learn something whether you're a beginner or an expert. And why not check out my book? Subscribe to the Mastering Emacs newsletter I write infrequently, so go on — sign up and receive an e-mail when I write new articles Email Address First Name Would you like to try a sample of Mastering Emacs for free ? Very interesting software, I've always felt there's something wrong with the current design of harnesses. I will give this a try in the next few days. I am curious about two things. First, would it be possible to make use of existing harnesses kernels ? Second, are you planning to release the source code ? — heiwiper · reply DreamCoder has its own internal tool loop system; it does not use other harnesses' kernels. That might be a thing in the future if there is enough demand for that. — ⭐ Mickey Petersen · reply so sad that browser is the best way to get cross platform gui, i generally hate applications that reinvent the window manager but this one is worth it. embark actions are an amazing solution i never found, i will be using those vehemently in my shithole projects. the "graph/visualization first" ui shape is i think the future of HITL harnesses. — Paths · reply I adore the slight skeumorphism in the UI design. Makes everything very legible. Flat design should never have happened at the scale it did, IMO. One nitpick: The download page misdetects the operating system, though, it detects Arch as Debian and tries to give me the Debian package. I suppose it can't do any better since all it gets from the user-agent header is "Linux". Gonna try the Docker release. — Psy-Q · reply > I adore the slight skeumorphism in the UI design. it's just a standard LLM-generated design these days: fonts, color palette, etc. No human touch at all. I'm disappointed. — DM13 · reply Really? Wow, the last few LLM designs I've seen were all terrible flat things full of pills and colored sidebars and whatnot, those were nothing special. This one I find super-easy to parse visually and even though it's colorful, it's not just rainbow barf. I wonder where the LLMs stole it, then? I haven't noticed any design movement going back to these ideas of raised buttons and bevels and whatnot, is this somehow inspired by the Frutiger Aero resurgence? — Psy-Q · reply Can you wrap the agents? We wrap our agents in Bubblewrap and give them very limited access to the filesystem. — Nebucatnetzer · reply Yes using a "shell command" hook. But note that DreamCoder itself has system access. Putting it in a container (there's a docker image for this) is even better. — ⭐ Mickey Petersen · reply It looks lovely, but sadly until it can use my Claude Code Max subscription I can't use it. (I assume I'm not missing something here?) — Gary · reply Hey Mickey, long time fan of your work, bought your book. Was briefly a combobulate user, but right when I was getting better at it, it was when the need to write code by hand went down by a large factor. I’ve been thinking so much about what would the “Emacs” of coding harnesses look like and been excited to see that Steve Yegge was using Emacs as an orchestrator and now DreamCoder as well. I feel that legendary Emacs users (as I consider yourselves to be) have great potential to shape the future of coding tools. Many people are discovering now the magic of being able to customize your tools while working with them. The Emacs community, however, already had the best system for that pre-AI. While many things might not transfer directly to this new world, so many lessons about customizable software, on how to build it, where it works, where it breaks, etc. Looking forward to see where you take DreamCoder! — Kao · reply Name Email Website C-x C-f is what command? title: Carnival Cruises emits ten times more sulphur oxide than all of Europe's cars (2019)
body_text: One corporation to pollute them all | Ecohustler Technology Nature Culture Rebel HQ Settings Achievements Sign Out Join Us Settings Achievements Sign Out Join Us Technology Nature Culture Search Newsletter SEARCH ECOHUSTLER POPULAR TOPICS Climate Change Renewable Energy Biodiversity Activism Rewilding WELCOME, REBEL Enter your credentials to access Rebel HQ ⚠️ EMAIL PASSWORD Remember me Forgot password? ENTER REBEL HQ Not a rebel yet? JOIN THE REBELLION → Technology One corporation to pollute them all Cruise giant - Carnival Corporation - emits 10 times more air pollution than all of Europe’s cars – study Team Ecohustler Publisher 16.06.2019 3 MIN READ SHARE: X FB LI SHARE X FB LI In April, Ecohustler disrupted Carnival Cruise's AGM calling on the shareholders to reduce their company's pollution using straight forward and affordable methods - like burning cleaner fuel. Since then, a new report outlines the corporation's impact on the coastline of Europe. These vast floating cities are burning dirty bunker fuel and creating shocking levels of air pollution wherever they go. Shipping has been an unregulated industry for too long and action is urgently required. Carnival Corporation, the world’s largest luxury cruise operator, emitted nearly 10 times more sulphur oxide (SOx) around European coasts than did all 260 million European cars in 2017, a new analysis by sustainable transport group Transport & Environment reveals. Royal Caribbean Cruises, the world’s second largest, is second, yet four times worse than the European car fleet. SOx emissions form sulphate (SO4) aerosols that increase human health risks and contribute to acidification in terrestrial and aquatic environments. SUPPORTED BY HEROES LIKE YOU Support independent eco journalism that drives real change. JOIN US → In absolute terms, Spain, Italy and Greece, closely followed by France and Norway, are the European countries most exposed to SOx air pollution from cruise vessels while Barcelona, Palma de Mallorca and Venice are the most impacted European port cities, followed by Civitavecchia (Rome) and Southampton. All photos by Greg English © These countries are so exposed because they are major tourist destinations, but also because they have less stringent marine sulphur fuel standards which allows cruise ships to burn the dirtiest most sulphurous fuel all along their coastlines. Faig Abbasov, shipping policy manager at T&E, said: “Luxury cruise ships are floating cities powered by some of the dirtiest fuel possible. Cities are rightly banning dirty diesel cars but they’re giving a free pass to cruise companies that spew out toxic fumes that do immeasurable harm both to those on board and on nearby shores. This is unacceptable.“ NOX emissions from cruise ships in Europe also heavily impact some cities, equivalent to about 15% of the nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted by Europe’s passenger car fleet in a year, the report finds. In Marseille, for example, 57 cruise ships emitted in 2017 almost as much NOx as one-quarter of the city’s 340,000 passenger cars. Along the coasts of countries such as Norway, Denmark, Greece, Croatia and Malta a handful of cruise ships are also responsible for more NOx than the majority of their domestic car fleet. Europe should implement a zero-emission port standard as soon as possible, this could then be extended to other ship types. The report also recommends extending emission control areas (ECAs), currently in place only in the North and Baltic Seas and English Channel, to the rest of the European seas. Furthermore, the report recommends regulating NOx emissions from existing ships, which are currently exempt from NOx standards applying in emission control areas. Faig Abbasov concluded “There are enough mature technologies to clean up cruise ships. Shore-side electricity can help cut in-port emissions, batteries are a solution for shorter distances and hydrogen technology can power even the biggest cruise ships. The cruise sector are apparently not willing to make the shift voluntarily, so we need governments to step in and mandate zero emission standards.” TAGGED: shipping Cruise Industry pollution corporations activism Stay connected with other changemakers. title: PostgreSQL 19
body_text: PostgreSQL: Release Notes Home About Download Documentation Community Developers Support Donate Your account November 19, 2026: PostgreSQL 19 Released! Quick Links Documentation Manuals Archive Release Notes Books Tutorials & Other Resources FAQ Wiki Release Notes PostgreSQL 19.0 E.1. Release 19 Prev   Up Appendix E. Release Notes Home   Next E.1. Release 19 # E.1.1. Overview E.1.2. Migration to Version 19 E.1.3. Changes E.1.4. Acknowledgments Release date:  2026-11-19 E.1.1. Overview # PostgreSQL 19 contains many new features and enhancements, including: New REPACK command that reclaims disk space and reorganizes table contents, which can improve query performance. REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) allows repacking without blocking reads and writes to the table. pg_plan_advice extension for controlling query planner decisions and pg_stash_advice extension that applies plan advice automatically based on the query. Better performance in many areas, including automatic scaling of the number of I/O worker processes, quicker foreign-key checks, and further planning and execution optimizations. Logical replication can now be enabled without a server restart when wal_level is set to replica . Logical replication of sequence values . Support for “ read-your-writes ” consistency on standbys via the new WAIT command. Parallel autovacuum of table indexes and autovacuum prioritization through a new scoring system. The above items and other new features of PostgreSQL 19 are explained in more detail in the sections below. E.1.2. Migration to Version 19 # A dump/restore using pg_dumpall or use of pg_upgrade or logical replication is required for those wishing to migrate data from any previous release. See Section 18.6 for general information on migrating to new major releases. Version 19 contains a number of changes that may affect compatibility with previous releases. Observe the following incompatibilities: Add server variable password_expiration_warning_threshold to warn about password expiration (Gilles Darold, Nathan Bossart) § The default warning period is seven days. Issue a warning after successful MD5 password authentication (Nathan Bossart) § The warning can be disabled via server variable md5_password_warnings . MD5 passwords were marked as deprecated in PostgreSQL 18. Remove RADIUS support (Thomas Munro) § PostgreSQL only supported RADIUS over UDP , which is unfixably insecure. Force standard_conforming_strings to always be on in the database server (Tom Lane) § Dumps created using pre- PostgreSQL 19 versions of pg_dump or pg_dumpall , and using standard_conforming_strings = off , will not properly load into PostgreSQL 19 and later servers. Users should create dumps using PostgreSQL 19 or later versions of these applications, or use standard_conforming_strings = on . Client applications still support operations with servers having standard_conforming_strings = off , for compatibility with old servers. The server variable escape_string_warning has been removed as unnecessary. Disallow carriage returns and line feeds in database, role, and tablespace names (Mahendra Singh Thalor) § pg_upgrade will also disallow upgrading of clusters that use such names. This was changed to avoid security problems. Change the default index opclasses for inet and cidr data types from btree_gist to GiST (Tom Lane) § § The btree_gist inet / cidr opclasses are broken because they can exclude rows that should be returned. pg_upgrade will disallow upgrading of clusters with btree_gist inet / cidr indexes. Disallow system columns from being used in COPY FROM ... WHERE (Tom Lane) § The values of such columns were not well-defined. Change a json_array() call which returns no rows to return an empty JSON array (Richard Guo) § This previously returned NULL . Cause transactions to pass their READ ONLY and DEFERRABLE status to postgres_fdw sessions (Etsuro Fujita) § This means READ ONLY transactions can no longer modify rows processed by postgres_fdw sessions. Change default of max_locks_per_transaction from 64 to 128 (Heikki Linnakangas) § Lock size allocation has changed, so effectively settings must now be doubled to match their capacity in previous releases. Remove server variable io_workers (Thomas Munro) § This has been replaced by four new variables; see Section E.1.3.1.2 . Change JIT to be disabled by default (Jelte Fennema-Nio) § Previously JIT was enabled by default, and activated based on optimizer costs, but this costing has been determined to be unreliable. This change requires sites that are doing many large analytical queries to manually enable JIT . Change parallel vacuum leaders and workers to share the cost-based vacuum delay limit (Bharath Rupireddy) § Previously each worker process slept based only on the cost it incurred itself, so a parallel vacuum could consume several times the budget set by vacuum_cost_limit . With this change, VACUUM with parallel workers and cost-based delay enabled might run slower than in previous releases. Rename column sync_error_count to sync_table_error_count in system view pg_stat_subscription_stats (Vignesh C) § This is necessary since sequence errors are now tracked separately. Rename wait event type BUFFERPIN to BUFFER and rename wait event BufferPin to BufferCleanup (Andres Freund) § Remove wait event BufferContent and add more precise wait events BufferShared , BufferShareExclusive , and BufferExclusive (Andres Freund) § Change index access method handlers to use a static IndexAmRoutines structure, rather than dynamically allocated ones (Matthias van de Meent) § Remove optimizer hook get_relation_info_hook and add better-placed hook build_simple_rel_hook (Robert Haas) § Change psql 's \crosstabview command to honor the \pset null setting (Chao Li) § Change full text search and pg_trgm to use the database's locale provider for character classification when parsing text (Jeff Davis) § Previously, characters were classified using libc, regardless of the locale provider. In databases with a locale provider other than libc (e.g., ICU , builtin ) and where the locale configured through that locale provider behaves differently from the LC_CTYPE setting configured for the database, particularly a LC_CTYPE of C , the output of some full text search and pg_trgm functions could change. When upgrading such databases using pg_upgrade , it is recommended to reindex all indexes which use full text search and pg_trgm after the upgrade, and to recompute any stored tsvector values. Change how fuzzystrmatch functions handle non- ASCII characters (Peter Eisentraut, Jeff Davis) § § dmetaphone() and dmetaphone_alt() now upper-case their input using the database's default collation rather than always using libc, and soundex() , metaphone() , and difference() now treat only ASCII letters as letters. When upgrading with pg_upgrade , it is recommended to reindex any indexes that use these functions after the upgrade. Remove MULE_INTERNAL encoding (Thomas Munro) § This encoding was complex and rarely used. Databases using it will need to be dumped and restored with a different encoding. E.1.3. Changes # Below you will find a detailed account of the changes between PostgreSQL 19 and the previous major release. E.1.3.1. Server # E.1.3.1.1. Optimizer # Allow NOT IN clauses to be converted to more efficient ANTI JOIN s when NULLs are not present (Richard Guo) § Allow more LEFT JOIN s to be converted to ANTI JOIN s (Tender Wang, Richard Guo) § Allow use of Memoize for ANTI JOIN s with unique inner sides (Richard Guo) § Allow some aggregate processing to be performed before joins (Richard Guo, Antonin Houska) § § § This can reduce the number of rows needed to be processed. Improve hash join's handling of tuples with NULL join keys (Tom Lane) § Improve the planning of semijoins (Richard Guo) § Allow Append and MergeAppend to consider explicit incremental sorts (Richard Guo) § Convert IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM NULL to IS [NOT] NULL during constant folding (Richard Guo) § The latter form is more easily optimized. Simplify IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM to equality/inequality operators when inputs are proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) § Perform earlier constant folding of var IS [NOT] NULL in the optimizer (Richard Guo) § This allows for later optimizations. Simplify COALESCE() and ROW(...) IS [NOT] NULL to avoid evaluating unnecessary arguments (Richard Guo) § § Simplify IS [NOT] TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN to plain boolean expressions when the input is proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) § Speed up join selectivity computations for large optimizer statistics targets (Ilia Evdokimov, David Geier) § Add proper optimizer statistics for functions returning boolean values (Tom Lane) § Allow extended statistics on virtual generated columns (Yugo Nagata) § Allow function pg_restore_extended_stats() to restore optimizer extended statistics (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier, Chao Li) § § § § Add function pg_clear_extended_stats() to remove extended statistics (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier) § Adjust the optimizer to consider startup costs of partial paths (Robert Haas, Tomas Vondra) § Allow negative values of pg_aggregate . aggtransspace to indicate unbounded memory usage (Richard Guo) § This information is used by the optimizer in planning memory usage. E.1.3.1.2. General Performance # Improve performance of foreign key constraint checks (Junwang Zhao, Amit Langote, Chao Li) § § Improve asynchronous I/O read-ahead scheduling for large requests (Andres Freund) § § § Allow io_method method worker to automatically control needed background workers (Thomas Munro) § The new server variables are io_min_workers , io_max_workers , io_worker_idle_timeout , and io_worker_launch_interval . Allow query table scans to mark pages as all-visible in the visibility map (Melanie Plageman) § Previously only VACUUM and COPY ... FREEZE could do this. Allow autovacuum to use parallel autovacuum workers (Daniil Davydov) § § The maximum number of workers is controlled by server variable autovacuum_max_parallel_workers and per-table storage parameter autovacuum_parallel_workers . Allow TID Range Scans to be parallelized (Cary Huang, David Rowley) § Improve COPY FROM performance for text and CSV input using SIMD CPU instructions (Nazir Bilal Yavuz, Shinya Kato) § Improve NOTIFY to only wake up backends that are listening to specified notifications (Joel Jacobson) § Previously most backends were woken by NOTIFY . Change wal_compression equals on to use the best WAL compression method available (wenhui qiu) § Previously this always used pglz . Change the default TOAST compression method from pglz to the more efficient lz4 (Euler Taveira) § This is done by changing the default for server variable default_toast_compression . Dismiss alert {{ message }} openssl openssl Repository navigation Code Issues 1k ( 1k ) Pull requests 682 ( 682 ) Discussions Actions Projects Wiki Security and quality Insights More items [NSF] [CVE-2026-121481] Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() - # 33652 # 33652 Open nmouha wants to merge 6 commits into openssl:master openssl/openssl:master from nmouha:cve-2026-121481 nmouha/openssl:cve-2026-121481 Copy head branch name to clipboard Conversation Commits 6 ( 6 ) Checks Files changed Open [NSF] [CVE-2026-121481] Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() # 33652 nmouha wants to merge 6 commits into openssl:master openssl/openssl:master from nmouha:cve-2026-121481 nmouha/openssl:cve-2026-121481 Copy head branch name to clipboard Conversation nmouha commented Nov 10, 2026 Copy link Copy Markdown Contributor This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" ( CVE-2026-121481 ) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock() : NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths for which the encoded size does not fit in an int . The OpenSSL SRT has asked for it to be fixed publicly; the advisory is still pending. Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock() . I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock() . No length limit is needed here because the decoded length always fits in an int , but it is a good idea to reject NULL buffers and negative lengths. Moreover, I propose to fix the incorrect length check in the base64encode() function of http_client.c , which rejected only len > INT_MAX . I am adding tests in test/base64_dec_avx2_test.c to cover the new behavior, and documenting the -1 returns in doc/man3/EVP_EncodeInit.pod . Exploiting this vulnerability from the command line is possible by passing a large -proxy_pass to openssl s_client . I confirmed that GOST accepts these large passwords out of the box. However, the password has to be supplied through an environment variable ( env:VAR ), otherwise the command line will be too long. Note: the pattern of CVE-2026-121481 is similar to that of CVE-2021-23840 . Checklist documentation is added or updated tests are added or updated --> Sorry, something went wrong. Uh oh! Both EVP_EncodeBlock() and EVP_DecodeBlock() can legitimately return 0, so 0 is not an error for either function. EVP_EncodeBlock() returns 0 when dlen == 0, and EVP_DecodeBlock() returns 0 when the input is empty after trimming. So, I wanted to make sure that both EVP_EncodeBlock() and EVP_DecodeBlock() consistently return -1 on any error. title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
body_text: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it · cekrem.github.io cekrem.github.io learnelm.dev Jesus!? About Recommended Books Podcast (🇳🇴) Blog If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it November 20, 2026 4-minute read AI • Software Craftsmanship • Coding-as-Craft Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty. It’s fine to read “Born to Run”, but you won’t be running an ultra marathon any time soon if you don’t start running. Whether it’s muscle memory, technique, physical fitness or problem solving you need to work on to reach your goals, you need to practice . This isn’t a controversial statement in any field at all , and has never really been. Except in software engineering, somehow. When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing . Making such a claim in any other field would be sneered at at best. Imagine John Scofield 1 saying he stopped practicing his guitar because “he was at a good enough level, musically, to maintain (and even improve!) his expertise” simply by 1) instructing others on how to play (either in vibe general terms, or with a strict spec musical notation), and then 2) listening to what they played and iterating until it sounded good enough for his next record. “My music is better”, he would claim, and moreover “actually playing the guitar was never the point anyway, there’s more to making music.” Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all. To make another comparison that’s arguably closer to software engineering, or at least the “writing and reasoning about code” part of it, let’s look at authors in other fields. I have no doubt that reading great prose has the potential to nudge a writer towards better writing of his/her own; in fact it’s super important to have creative references to draw upon - no doubt at all. But, imagine an author who 1) stopped writing, and only pursued reading and giving feedback to other writers, and worse yet 2) mostly read AI generated prose !? To be perfectly honest, I would expect a quite steady (if not exponential) decline of this author’s writing skills. “There’s more to software engineering than writing code” Link to heading Sure. But if we can at least agree that the code that runs our software is a non-trivial part of it (though, granted, not all of it by far: The other parts of developing and maintaining software speak even louder against using generative AI as a significant tool service! ), we should aspire to be proficient in understanding how code works, what good code looks like, what to watch out for and how software architecture plays a vital part in making code Easy To Change. Simply “reviewing all the code Claude produced” won’t quite cut it. And who are you trying to fool, after all; at this point you’re not really reading half of it, are you? So I propose something that used to be a no-brainer: Keep practicing! Which brings me to my next point: All engineers(!) need to be good at solving problems Link to heading if || while you can argue that the need for being hands-on on your software’s code varies, I propose you can’t argue that we’re still solving problems . And the moment you stop practicing solving problems is the moment you stop getting better at it, just like everything else. Simple as that. This is hardly new, btw: you could always tell who beat Doom using cheat codes and who finished the game the real way! If the end goal is to “beat the game”, then by all means cheat; if the end goal is getting good at it , then I’d advice you not to. Some lessons are only learned the hard way (trial and error ), and very few are learned without effort at all . Repeated LLM usage for problem solving pounds the following premise into our brain’s wiring: If something is hard, tricky or requires effort, you shouldn’t even try. And right there goes our learning, craft and joy, right out the window. In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy , I don’t want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline , I can’t help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea . It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all? — Em’s blog 2 , emphasis mine. Please, John Scofield, don’t stop playing your guitar!   ↩︎ I’m not sure who Em is, but their blog is great!  ↩︎ © 2021 - 2026 Christian Ekrem
